title: Psychological Safety
subtitle: What happens after someone asks a question, admits a mistake or disagrees, and how to make that moment useful
summary: A useful question can improve the work, yet asking it can carry a social risk. This course builds psychological safety as the readings define it: a team's shared expectation that asking, admitting an error, raising a concern or disagreeing will be examined rather than ridiculed or punished. It is not comfort, niceness or lower standards. You practice raising a precise question, receiving one about your own work, handling a mistake in the present and learning from it, leading repair when you hold more power, and knowing where team habits end and formal routes begin. A workplace simulation lets you try these moves when a newer colleague's question gets brushed aside in a team huddle.
objectives: Explain psychological safety as a shared team expectation about interpersonal risk, and say what it is not: comfort, agreement, lower standards or a promise of secrecy.
Describe how position, earlier responses and different meanings of speaking up can change the cost of a question, without inferring anyone's experience from a group.
Raise a concern as an observation, a task consequence and a specific request, and receive a question about your own work by examining it before defending it.
Respond to a mistake by addressing the present need first, then examining conditions and choices without public blame or promises that no one is responsible.
Distinguish team learning from formal respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination routes, including prompt DHS employee reporting and the immediate duty of managers and supervisors.

narrator.voice_notes: Warm, measured professional delivery. Read the connected explanations naturally, leaving room around questions and examples. Preserve the selected voice identities and the exact meaning of policy boundaries.

segments.title: Why an ordinary question carries risk

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Psychological Safety. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer with a warm, open expression, hands loosely clasped.
on_screen: What happens after someone asks, admits a mistake or disagrees
scenes.narration: Welcome to Psychological Safety. Consider a recent moment when you had a question at work but decided to keep it to yourself. Perhaps the meeting was moving quickly, or the person you needed to question had considerable influence over your next assignment. Holding back may have seemed reasonable, especially if you expected your question to be taken as evidence that you were unprepared. This course examines those expectations and the responses that strengthen or change them when someone does decide to speak. Psychological safety concerns what people expect will happen when they ask questions, acknowledge mistakes, raise concerns or disagree with colleagues. In DHS work, those expectations can affect whether important information reaches a service decision, a policy review or an incident debrief. You will examine why the risk differs across working relationships, practice raising and receiving questions, and explore the consequences through a workplace simulation.

“Could this instruction leave someone without a usable route?”
scenes.narration: One reading begins with a colleague asking, “Could this instruction leave someone without a usable route?” The response is, “We have already discussed that.” The reply establishes that a discussion occurred, but it provides no explanation of what was considered or how the concern was resolved. The colleague may need a reference, a correction or a clearer account of which conditions the instruction is intended to cover. Without that information, the exchange can discourage another question while leaving the practical uncertainty exactly where it began. Repeated responses of this kind may teach people to withhold information that would help the team examine its work. That possibility is worth investigating, although one exchange cannot establish how every person experiences the team. Begin with the observable response and the unanswered work question, rather than assigning a motive or diagnosing the whole workplace.

scenes.narration: Amy Edmondson's research helps explain why the number of reported problems can be difficult to interpret without understanding the team. In her hospital research, teams that appeared to work better together sometimes reported more errors, prompting closer examination of reporting behavior. A higher count could reflect greater willingness to discuss errors rather than a higher underlying rate of mistakes. The practical implication is that silence can conceal information leaders need, while candid discussion can make problems available for examination. In DHS service reviews and incident debriefs, that distinction matters because unresolved problems may affect people who rely on the service. A team needs to understand both what happened and whether its usual responses encourage staff to report what they notice. Consider where someone might hesitate before reporting an error, and what information the person responsible would lose if that concern remained unspoken.

on_screen: How disagreement and mistakes are handled
Who carries repair, and whether input changes anything
scenes.narration: The program reading on psychological safety and repair describes concerns within the Disability Services Division about pressure and whether staff input changes decisions. That account provides context for the reading; it does not describe every current DSD team or establish conditions across the agency. Its central point is that these concerns call for changes in how people respond at work, rather than asking staff to become braver. A team can look at how it handles disagreement, what happens after a mistake and who takes the lead when a response causes harm. It can also check whether staff input reaches the people making decisions and whether those contributions receive an answer that addresses the question. These practices give colleagues something specific to discuss and improve within their roles, even when their views of the team's overall climate differ.

on_screen: What it is, and why the risk differs
Asking, receiving, mistakes and formal routes
scenes.narration: The course begins by distinguishing psychological safety from comfort, agreement and an absence of professional accountability. It then examines how position, prior experience and the available ways to contribute can change the risk of speaking up. You will practice raising a precise work question and receiving a question about something you have prepared or decided. The following sections address mistakes, repair and the boundary between everyday team habits and required formal reporting procedures. Reflection questions provide opportunities to connect those ideas with your own work or discuss an example with a trusted colleague. As you begin, bring to mind a time when you held back a question or received one that felt difficult to hear. Returning to that moment throughout the course can help you identify a response you would approach differently and explain why.

check.prompt: A colleague asks whether an instruction could leave someone without a usable route. The reply is, “We have already discussed that.” What does the reply leave open?

options.text: It says a discussion happened but not what it settled, so the colleague's work question is still unanswered and the next person may think twice before asking.

feedback.text: You kept the work question in view and noticed what the reply teaches. Build on that by asking what the earlier discussion actually established.
Next time you hear a reply like that, try: “What did that discussion settle? I want to make sure this case is covered.”

options.text: Very little, since the team already talked it through, and reopening old discussions every time someone asks can slow the work down for everyone else in the meeting.

feedback.text: Protecting meeting time is a real concern, and repeating old debates can drain a team. The catch is that the reply never showed what the earlier talk decided, so the question stays open.

The reply leaves the substance of the earlier decision unclear. Point to what was settled and check whether it covers this case, rather than assume a brief reference always answers the current question.

options.text: It shows the person who replied does not care about access, so that attitude should be raised with their supervisor before the instruction itself is looked at.

feedback.text: The reply shows a brush-off, not a motive. A stronger response stays with what can be seen: the question is unanswered. That keeps attention on the instruction.
What would you need to see before concluding what someone cares about?

reflection: Think of a question you held back at work. What did you expect would happen if you asked it?
What reply have you heard, or given, that answered a question with a shortcut instead of an explanation?
Where in your work could an unasked question become a problem for the people you serve?

segments.title: What psychological safety is and is not

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A shared belief about risk. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands relaxed at his sides.
on_screen: A team condition, not a personality trait
scenes.narration: Edmondson describes team psychological safety as a shared expectation that members can take interpersonal risks within their working group. Those risks include asking for help, acknowledging an error or questioning a proposal when doing so might affect how colleagues judge you. The concept concerns the team's response to these ordinary work acts, rather than an individual's confidence or willingness to challenge authority. A knowledgeable employee may still withhold a question if earlier questions have been met with ridicule or dismissal. Someone who speaks readily may also encounter different consequences from a colleague with less influence over the same decision. To examine psychological safety, consider what people expect from the group and what actually happens when a question is raised. That focus directs attention toward working conditions the team can change, rather than treating courage as a personal requirement for participation.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What the research shows. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, gesturing toward the first point.
scenes.narration: Edmondson's 1999 study examined fifty-one work teams in a manufacturing company and compared psychological safety with the ways those teams learned. Teams reporting greater safety also described more learning behavior, such as asking for help, discussing errors and raising questions about uncertain work. Learning behavior was also linked with team performance, giving researchers a reason to examine how working relationships can support better results. These findings show links in the study; they do not prove that one response will cause a certain outcome in another workplace. Applying the ideas at DHS requires a close look at the team's actual tasks, roles and conditions before drawing conclusions about its work. The study cannot certify that a DHS team is safe, and it offers no basis for judging an individual employee. Use it to ask careful questions about how colleagues share information and respond when something needs a closer look.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Not niceness, not low standards. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand raised slightly, palm out.
on_screen: Candor is how standards get met
scenes.narration: Psychological safety makes room for candid discussion of demanding work, including conversations that may feel uncomfortable to the people taking part. In The Fearless Organization, Edmondson brings the ability to speak openly together with high expectations for the work and for people's conduct. A team can require sound decisions and careful preparation while still welcoming someone who says that a detail is unclear or wrong. Her account of organizations such as Pixar presents candid review as part of producing quality, rather than a reason to lower standards. The question is whether people can raise a real concern without being shamed or punished simply for drawing attention to it. That expectation does not excuse misconduct or mean that every claim should be accepted without checking the evidence behind it. Clear standards and a useful response to questions help colleagues address problems together instead of hiding them to protect appearances.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A calm meeting proves little. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, head tilted slightly, thoughtful.
on_screen: Agreement is not evidence of safety
scenes.narration: A meeting with no objections can appear successful, particularly when a team is working under pressure to reach a decision. Yet silence could reflect shared understanding, limited opportunity to contribute or uncertainty about how a question would be received. The meeting record alone does not establish which explanation applies, even when everyone appeared to agree at the time. Supported agreement can help the work progress, but it does not show how the team would respond to a substantive challenge. Similarly, a difficult discussion may involve productive examination of a problem rather than evidence that learning has become impossible. Look beyond the atmosphere to the way a specific question is handled and the information available to resolve it. This gives the team something concrete to examine without treating either calm or conflict as a reliable measure on its own.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Disagreement is not disrespect. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, holding up two fingers as if counting two separate questions.
scenes.narration: A useful review allows colleagues to challenge a conclusion while treating each other with respect throughout the discussion and its follow-up. Minnesota Management and Budget's Respectful Workplace policy, Policy 1432, distinguishes normal work activities from conduct that fails to meet that expectation. A difference of opinion or routine direction from a supervisor is not, by itself, evidence that someone has broken the policy. At the same time, raising an important work concern does not excuse threats, bullying or demeaning treatment of another person. Keep the two questions distinct: is the claim supported by evidence, and did the way people spoke to each other meet workplace expectations? A respectful colleague can be wrong, while someone who has found a real problem can still respond in a harmful way. Addressing one issue does not settle the other; use the agency's process when you need help deciding how the policy applies.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What it does not promise. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, shaking his head gently, a slight smile.
on_screen: Not secrecy, not freedom from accountability
scenes.narration: An invitation to speak becomes less credible when it promises results that the person making the promise has no power to deliver. Accepting every idea, keeping everything in the room or setting aside workplace standards would go beyond what psychological safety means. Ideas still need evidence, someone still has responsibility for the decision, and some concerns must be reported through a formal process. A useful invitation explains what remains open, how comments will be considered and which duties limit what can be kept private. Colleagues can then choose how to take part with a clearer understanding of what they can expect from the invitation. The readings also distinguish a team's ability to raise concerns from cultural safety and from the agency's formal reporting and response systems. These ideas may inform one another, but one meeting or survey cannot show that all three are working as intended.

check.prompt: Which statement fits psychological safety as the readings describe it?

options.text: A team expects that asking, admitting an error or disagreeing will not bring humiliation, while standards, evidence and formal duties all stay in place.

feedback.text: You held both halves together: room to take an ordinary risk, and standards that still apply. Build on it by noticing which half your team tends to drop under pressure.
On your team, what usually happens to the first person who disagrees?

options.text: A team where people feel comfortable and conflict stays low, because members trust each other enough that hard feedback is rarely needed to get the work done well.

feedback.text: Many people picture safety as comfort, and a calm team can feel safe. The readings frame it differently: safety makes hard feedback possible rather than unnecessary.
Compare this with high safety and high expectations. A team can be candid and demanding at once. Low conflict on its own says little about what happens to a question.

options.text: A promise from the leader that every concern raised inside the team stays inside the team, so people can speak without worrying about what might follow.

feedback.text: That promise goes beyond any leader's authority. Some concerns a supervisor has to route formally. A stronger invitation explains what is open and what has to go elsewhere.
Picture the person who later learns their concern had to be reported after all. An honest limit at the start would have served them better than a promise.

options.text: A trait that confident employees bring with them, which is why some people on a team speak up easily in meetings while others usually stay quiet.

feedback.text: Edmondson describes a team condition, not a personality trait. The useful question is how the team responds to a risk, not who is naturally bold.
When someone is quiet, try looking at the conditions first: how was the last question received, and was there another way to contribute?

reflection: Think of a team where you felt free to disagree. What did the leader or the group do that made that possible?
Where have you seen kindness used as a reason to skip hard feedback?
What promise about safety have you heard that went further than anyone could keep?

segments.title: Why the risk is not the same for everyone

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: The cost of asking differs. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands loosely clasped.
on_screen: Silence is not evidence of no concern
scenes.narration: An invitation to ask questions can carry different consequences for people attending the same meeting and considering the same proposal. A long-serving colleague and someone in their first month may have different expectations about how a challenge will affect their working relationships. Position, earlier responses to questions, visibility and access to support can all influence whether contributing feels worthwhile or carries a personal cost. Those conditions deserve attention, but they do not establish what any particular colleague thinks or explain every instance of silence. Avoid treating quiet participation as evidence of agreement, limited knowledge or a fixed reluctance to speak in a group. Instead, examine how the team provides opportunities to contribute and what happens when someone uses one of those opportunities. Repeatedly asking the person with the least influence to become more confident can leave the conditions creating the risk entirely unchanged.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: An open door is not enough. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one arm extended slightly as if holding a door open.
on_screen: An open door is not enough
The person inviting input may control assignments
Pair the door with usable routes
scenes.narration: An open-door invitation is useful when the experience of raising a concern supports the promise that someone will receive it seriously. The leader offering that invitation may also influence assignments, evaluations and development opportunities, which staff can reasonably consider before disagreeing. In one practice case, a temporary staff member notices an access problem in a form prepared under a project lead's direction. She worries that challenging the lead publicly could affect future assignments, even though the form still needs a substantive review. A prepared written question or a private conversation may provide a workable way to contribute the information before a decision is made. The team should not require her to explain personal experiences before making that route available or examining the concern. A leader who receives no visits therefore needs more evidence before concluding that everyone understands the work or has no concerns.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Who bears the cost. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, serious and calm, hands at her sides.
on_screen: A climate that punishes candor silences some people first
scenes.narration: The program reading of The Fearless Organization asks readers to consider who bears the greatest cost when a workplace discourages candor. Its discussion of inclusion emphasizes that staff from underrepresented groups may encounter additional consequences when questioning an established practice or decision. The reading also critiques approaches that concentrate on team interaction without sufficiently examining power and identity, and it recommends considering those conditions together. This is a question about how a workplace operates, rather than permission to infer an individual's experience from group membership. Colleagues who share an identity may describe different experiences, and no person should be expected to represent everyone with that identity. To examine the issue, ask how people can contribute, how their concerns are received and what they themselves report about those conditions. Keep the scope of each account clear instead of replacing inquiry with an assumption about who feels safe.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two ways of caring. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, both hands open, one slightly higher than the other, as if weighing two things.
on_screen: A quick question can be active care
A prepared question can be respect
scenes.narration: A practice story follows two colleagues reviewing a draft whose different ways of contributing initially lead them to misread one another. One asks questions as the document is read aloud, while the other prefers to review the wording before sending a prepared question. The first interprets the delay as reluctance to challenge the team; the second experiences the immediate questions as putting colleagues on the spot. When they discuss their habits, the first explains that asking promptly shows care because a problem can still be addressed together. The second explains that arriving with a considered question respects other people's preparation and protects the quality of the working relationship. Both are trying to contribute responsibly, although their visible behavior communicates a different meaning to the person watching it. Their explanations belong to these two colleagues and do not establish a rule about a culture, community or type of employee.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Widen the frame, then change the response. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, gesturing outward with both hands.
on_screen: Widen the frame, then change the response
Offer more than one way in
scenes.narration: The practical response to different ways of contributing is to arrange the work so that relevant information can reach the decision. Name the question that remains open, explain when a response is needed and provide a way to contribute a prepared comment. A written route is useful only if someone receives the contribution, examines it and brings it to the person responsible before the decision closes. A comment box that nobody reads offers the appearance of choice while leaving the team's knowledge no better than before. Likewise, moving a question out of a meeting requires a clear next step so that the contribution does not disappear afterward. Consider which signals you tend to reward, such as speed, certainty, preparation or direct challenge, and whether those preferences affect whose contribution is examined. The aim is to improve access to the work discussion while retaining a clear decision process.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Contribution without disclosure. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand resting lightly over her heart.
on_screen: No one speaks for a whole group
scenes.narration: A concern about a form or process should receive attention without requiring the person to share painful experiences to explain why it matters. Belonging to a community also does not make someone responsible for explaining that community or teaching colleagues about every related issue. Ask for the facts or perspective needed to examine the work, and explain why that information would help resolve the question. The person can then contribute without having to defend the concern through a personal history or an account of their identity. If someone chooses to share more, listen carefully and avoid treating that choice as permission to repeat their story elsewhere. Explain any duty to report what you hear, rather than making a promise that everything will remain between the two of you. This approach keeps the work question open while respecting the person's choices about what else they wish to share.

check.prompt: A newer colleague rarely speaks in team meetings but sends careful written questions afterward. Which response fits the readings best?

options.text: Make sure written questions reach the person deciding before the choice closes, and do not read the colleague's quiet in meetings as low confidence or commitment.

feedback.text: You treated the written questions as real contributions and made sure they can still matter. Build on it by telling the team when written input is due and who reads it.
To the colleague, a prepared question may be the respectful way to contribute. Seeing it reach the decision tells them the route is real.

options.text: Encourage the colleague to raise questions in the room next time, since live questions get discussed by everyone and their good ideas deserve more visibility on the team.

feedback.text: An invitation to speak in meetings can be useful when it does not discount written contributions. The priority here is checking that the existing written route reaches the decision in time.

Clarify when input is needed and who reviews it, while keeping both written and spoken contributions available where the work allows. Ask the colleague about the arrangement rather than deciding what their quietness means.

options.text: Ask the colleague what in their background makes speaking in meetings hard for them, so the team can adjust the way it runs meetings to fit their culture better.

feedback.text: This asks for a personal story and assumes the reason is cultural. A stronger move asks what would make contributing easier, without needing to know why.
Try instead: “Your written questions have been useful. Is there anything about how the team takes input that would make it easier for you?”

reflection: Who on your team has the most influence over other people's assignments? How might that shape what gets said in the room?
Which signal of engagement do you tend to reward: speed, certainty, preparation or direct challenge?
If you wanted to know whether everyone on your team can raise concerns equally, how would you find out without guessing?

segments.title: Raising a question and receiving one

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Make the question examinable. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the royal blue blouse (C5), playing the team member in the reading's story, stands full length, holding a printed page and pointing to a line on it.
on_screen: “This paragraph names only the web contact.”
scenes.narration: A precise concern helps colleagues identify what needs examination and distinguish the evidence from an interpretation of someone else's intentions. One reading suggests naming the observation, explaining its possible effect on the task and asking for the clarification or action needed. In its practice story, a team member notices that a source lists two contact options while the draft notice includes only the web contact. Saying that someone is hiding an access problem would add a motive that the available material does not establish. Instead, she points to the paragraph, identifies the additional option in the source and asks which contact arrangements apply to this notice. That question gives the person responsible a specific discrepancy to examine against the applicable conditions and approved wording. The approach keeps attention on whether the notice will work for its intended audience, while leaving room for an explanation the reviewer has not yet seen.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Honest about what you do not know. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand raised slightly in a modest, open gesture.
on_screen: Honest about what you do not know
Precision helps; polish is not the price of an answer
scenes.narration: Naming uncertainty can make a concern easier to examine without withdrawing the substance of what you have observed. Saying that you may be missing a condition invites a check; telling colleagues to ignore you because you are probably wrong erases the question. Neither exaggerated certainty nor an apology that dismisses your own observation improves the evidence available to the team. At the same time, a well-phrased question should not become a requirement that someone must meet before receiving a serious response. People under pressure may describe a real problem in broad or frustrated language, leaving the receiver to ask for a concrete example. A statement that nobody cares about access is harder to examine than a missing contact instruction, but it may point toward the same problem. Hear the substance, clarify what happened and help turn the concern into a question that the responsible person can address.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Within your role. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand gesturing to the side as if passing something along.
on_screen: Bring the question to the person responsible
You do not have to become the final authority
scenes.narration: Choose a route that can bring the concern to someone with responsibility for the decision or the information needed to resolve it. If the draft's author is present, identifying the paragraph may allow the team to examine the question immediately. If interpreting a condition belongs to another role, explain that dependency and help the question reach the person who can answer it. You do not need to become the final policy authority or promise a correction that you have no authority to approve. A clear recipient and an agreed next step are more useful than copying many people without establishing who will respond. Remember that effective communication is a shared responsibility: a precise question can still encounter a dismissive or unhelpful response. Improving the way a concern is raised therefore needs to be accompanied by attention to how the team receives and resolves it.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: When someone questions your work. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the white blouse with curly hair (C3), playing the experienced colleague in the reading's story, stands full length, holding a thick folder against her chest, mid-thought.
on_screen: “What next step does it suggest to you?”
scenes.narration: Receiving a question about your own work can feel different from examining the same issue in a document prepared by someone else. In a practice story, an experienced colleague has invested considerable care in a draft when a newer colleague questions the next contact step. The experienced colleague feels that the effort behind the document has been overlooked and begins to respond by pointing to the newcomer's limited experience. Length of service may provide useful background, but it cannot establish whether this particular sentence communicates the intended instruction accurately. A more useful opening acknowledges the sentence and asks what next step the newer colleague understood it to require. That response gathers information about how the wording reads before defending the reasoning that produced it. The draft may ultimately be correct, but examining the interpretation gives both colleagues evidence with which to assess it.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Recognition is not agreement. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, counting on his fingers.
on_screen: A receipt is not an answer
scenes.narration: Taking a question seriously means examining it and providing a usable response, without assuming that the proposed change must be accepted. After checking the source, you may explain why the existing wording is accurate, revise it through the appropriate review or identify a condition another role must settle. Each outcome can respect the contribution when the reasoning is clear and the person knows what happened to the question. A warm acknowledgment followed by no examination leaves the work unresolved, even if the exchange sounds welcoming on the surface. Explain what you found, or identify who is checking the condition and how the answer will return to the people who need it. An acknowledgment that a message was received establishes delivery; it does not show that the underlying concern has been answered. Following through makes the invitation to question the work credible in practice.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Do not ask for reassurance. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, hands in a calm, steady position at his waist.
on_screen: Good intentions do not answer the question
No loyalty test before the work
scenes.narration: When feedback feels personal, explaining your intention may seem like the quickest way to restore a comfortable working relationship. Yet wanting to help does not establish whether the instruction, response or decision actually worked for the person affected. If a conversation repeatedly turns toward reassuring the receiver, colleagues may learn that raising a concern creates additional emotional work for them. Avoid making agreement, loyalty or a personal explanation the condition for examining a question about the work itself. Instead, notice whether status, confidence or preparation changes how readily you treat a question as useful rather than disrespectful. A clarifying question can create enough room to understand the concern before you explain the reasoning behind your original response. You can then consider intention alongside the observed effect, without asking the other person to settle your discomfort before the work receives attention.

check.prompt: A new colleague asks whether a sentence in your draft explains the next contact step correctly. You are fairly sure it does. What is the most useful first response?

options.text: Thank them for pointing to the sentence, ask what next step it suggests to them, and compare it with the current source before you explain what you find.

feedback.text: You stayed open even though you expected to be right. That keeps the question about the sentence, not about either of you. Build on it by telling them what you found.
If the source backs you up, try: “Here is the condition it follows. Does that make the sentence clearer, or should the wording change?”

options.text: Walk them through the background behind the wording and how long the team has used it, so they can see why the sentence reads the way it does now.

feedback.text: Explaining the background is a natural, helpful instinct, especially with someone new. The gap is that history shows how the sentence came to be, not whether it reads clearly today.
A stronger first move asks how the sentence reads to them. Then the background can answer the actual confusion instead of a guessed one.

options.text: Tell them it is a great question and you appreciate them speaking up, then keep the sentence as written, since you are fairly sure it is right.

feedback.text: The thanks is warm, but the sentence never gets examined. Recognition works best as the start of a check, not a replacement for one.
To the new colleague, praise followed by no change and no explanation can feel like a polite way of closing the door.

options.text: Change the sentence right away to match their reading, since a new person's confusion is enough evidence that the wording is not working for anyone reading it.

feedback.text: Welcoming the question does not settle its answer. A stronger move checks the source first, then changes the wording if the check supports it.
What would you want to know before deciding the sentence is wrong for everyone?

reflection: Think of a concern you raised that turned into a debate about motives. How could you have named only what you observed?
When someone questions your work, what is your first reaction? What clarifying question could you ask before explaining?
Where have you seen a friendly acknowledgment stand in for an actual answer?

segments.title: Mistakes and repair

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A mistake needs a present response. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, facing the viewer, steady and calm.
on_screen: A mistake needs a present response
Correct it, then examine how it happened
scenes.narration: A service message containing an incorrect date creates an immediate problem for its readers and a separate question about how the error occurred. The person responsible may need to correct the message promptly so that people do not rely on information the team knows is wrong. Once that need is addressed, the review can examine the source, the preparation process and the checks that preceded release. Calling the employee careless may overlook an unclear source or a review step that failed to identify the discrepancy. Declaring that mistakes do not matter would overlook the effect on people arranging their time or seeking a service. A useful response holds both responsibilities together: address the present problem and examine the conditions and choices that contributed to it. This approach allows learning without treating either personal blame or reassurance as a substitute for correcting the work.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A future meeting cannot fix today. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the navy polo (C4), playing the team member in the reading's story, stands full length, holding a large envelope, looking at it with a slight frown.
on_screen: A future meeting cannot fix today
Supply what the receiver needs now
scenes.narration: In another practice story, a team member sends a review package without the source attachment needed to check a condition. The receiver returns the package because the missing information prevents the review from proceeding, delaying work that depends on the answer. Offering to discuss the mistake at a future learning meeting may be useful, but it does not supply what the receiver needs now. The sender first needs to provide the source and clarify any immediate effect on the review schedule or dependent work. Examination then reveals that the checklist covered the draft but omitted the source, while the sender assumed the receiver could locate it independently. Adding the required source to the checklist addresses a specific weakness that another reviewer can recognize and use. A promise never to make another mistake cannot provide the same practical assurance or show how the process has improved.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two shortcuts to avoid. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand lifted toward each point in turn.
scenes.narration: Teams under pressure may respond to an error by naming a person to blame or declaring that the system alone caused it. Public blame can produce a quick explanation while discouraging disclosure and leaving weaknesses in the process insufficiently examined. A blanket statement that nobody is responsible can also obscure the choices involved and leave the next corrective task without a clear owner. Neither response provides the careful account needed to understand what happened and determine which changes are within the team's authority. Examine the conditions and individual decisions together, using the available evidence rather than deciding the explanation in advance. Identify who will correct the work and what support or review is required to make that correction dependable. Any personnel or other formal matter should follow its appropriate process, rather than being decided through a team learning conversation.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Repair sits with more power. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, serious, hands loosely clasped in front.
on_screen: No explaining or forgiving on a schedule
scenes.narration: Repair also concerns how colleagues are treated when a comment or decision dismisses their contribution or causes harm in a working relationship. The reading asks the person with greater power to take responsibility for the response, rather than waiting for the affected person to initiate repair. A leader can name what happened, acknowledge their part and explain what will change without demanding reassurance or forgiveness. Information and a genuine opportunity to change may help when misunderstanding contributed to the problem, but they do not erase its effect. Nor does an explanation that harm was unintentional determine whether a reporting duty or formal process applies. Required reporting must proceed according to policy, without waiting for the person to prove intent or complete a repair conversation. The aim is to address the response within your authority while preserving the responsibilities that belong to the formal process.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Repair in the same setting. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8), playing the supervisor in the reading's story, stands full length, facing the viewer as if addressing a team, one hand open.
on_screen: Credit the concern and say you should have listened
scenes.narration: A supervisor in a policy team dismisses a newer analyst's concern that a notice may confuse families, saying there is no time to revisit it. Two weeks later, a county partner identifies the same problem, and the supervisor notices that the analyst has stopped contributing in meetings. Asking him privately to speak more would place the burden on the colleague whose earlier contribution was dismissed. In the reading's stronger response, the supervisor acknowledges at the next team meeting that the analyst raised the concern first and should have received a substantive answer. She explains what will change in the notice and how she will respond when colleagues raise similar questions in future. Because the original concern and dismissal occurred in the meeting, that setting allows the team to hear the correction. When a concern was raised privately, ask before identifying its contributor publicly, so that recognition does not create an unwanted disclosure.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Repair your own response. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse with locs (C2) stands full length, one hand on her chest, the other open toward the viewer.
on_screen: Check where your first reading traveled
scenes.narration: You can repair an unhelpful response within your own responsibilities even when you do not supervise or manage anyone. If you dismissed a relevant question, acknowledge the response directly and explain how the question will receive an answer now. That commitment gives the colleague something practical to assess, without asking them to confirm that the relationship or experience is already resolved. An apology may matter while leaving the other person's interpretation, feelings and choices entirely their own to describe. Also consider whether your initial interpretation traveled into a note, a summary or another person's assessment of the colleague's work. A private change of mind will not automatically correct a label that has already influenced someone else's understanding or decision. Identify what you can correct through the proper process, and distinguish that action from promising an outcome outside your authority.

check.prompt: A teammate realizes a notice went out with an outdated date. The team lead wants to handle it well. Which response fits the readings best?

options.text: Correct the date through the person responsible now, then look at how the old date got in and past review, keeping any formal matter separate.

feedback.text: You began the correction and examined how the error reached the notice. Confirm that affected recipients receive the verified information, then test any process change without assuming distribution alone resolves every consequence.
A factual review can acknowledge the value of reporting while retaining accountability. Its effect on future reporting needs observation rather than a guarantee about how the teammate will respond.

options.text: Put the error on the agenda for next month's team learning review, so the whole team can examine it together without anyone feeling singled out in the moment.

feedback.text: Wanting to learn as a team without singling anyone out is a good instinct. The catch is timing: the people who got the wrong date need a correction now, not next month.
Try doing both: correct the notice today, then bring the how-it-happened question to the review.

options.text: Reassure the teammate that nobody is responsible because the process caused it, so that people across the team feel safe admitting mistakes in the future.

feedback.text: The process may have played a part, but declaring that nobody is responsible goes beyond what a lead can promise and can leave the fix with no owner.
How could you name the process gap and still keep the next step owned by someone?

options.text: Name the teammate in the team meeting so the cause is clear, then ask everyone to check their work more carefully from now on.

feedback.text: Public blame gives a quick explanation but can hide the step that let the date through. A stronger response corrects the notice and examines the review process.

Naming a colleague as the explanation leaves the process gap unexamined. Share the information needed for learning and follow the applicable personnel and privacy requirements without unnecessary public attribution.

reflection: When a mistake surfaces on your team, which shortcut is more tempting: blame, or declaring that nobody is responsible?
Think of a time your response cut someone off. Where did that first reading travel, and could any of it still be corrected?
Where do you hold more power than the people around you, and what would leading a repair look like there?

segments.title: Team habits and formal routes

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three layers. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand held flat, raised in steps as if marking levels.
on_screen: Law sets the floor; policy sets a higher standard
You do not have to classify it first
scenes.narration: Team habits can help concerns surface, but they do not replace agency procedures for discrimination, harassment or disrespectful conduct. Federal and Minnesota law provide legal protections, while state and DHS policies also set expectations and duties in the workplace. Policy 1436 addresses protected-class harassment and discrimination; Policy 1432 covers disrespectful conduct outside its exclusions for protected-class and sexual harassment. Demeaning remarks or misuse of someone's name need to be considered in context, rather than sorted into a category from a brief example alone. You do not have to decide which policy was violated before raising a concern through an available reporting route. Human Resources and the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division can explain which process applies and what each person needs to do. Provide a factual account through those routes instead of using a team discussion to investigate the concern or decide its outcome.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: If you see it happen. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand open, fingers spread as if counting five.
on_screen: Ask the targeted person what they want
scenes.narration: Right To Be describes five ways to support someone who is experiencing harassment, with attention to safety and avoiding escalation. Distract means interrupting indirectly, while Delegate means asking someone else to help respond to what you have seen or heard. Document means making an accurate record, and Delay means checking in afterward when you were unable to help at the time. Direct means naming the behavior briefly when it is safe to do so and unlikely to make the situation worse. These choices can help a person in the moment, but they do not replace reporting duties that apply to your DHS role. Ask what the person wants done with notes or other documentation, while explaining any duty to share information through an agency process. Do not circulate their experience for general discussion or promise that their wishes override every duty to report a concern.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: If someone brings you a concern. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, leaning in slightly, listening.
on_screen: If someone brings you a concern
Listen, thank them, share the routes
scenes.narration: When a colleague brings you a concern, listen carefully and explain your role before promising to keep anything between the two of you. DHS policy expects employees to promptly report discrimination, harassment or retaliation complaints to a supervisor or Equal Opportunity and Access. Those reporting routes and Human Resources can help determine which agency process applies to the concern and what happens next. A union representative or the Employee Assistance Program can offer support, but seeking support does not necessarily make a report to the agency. External routes include the Minnesota Department of Human Rights and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which each have their own procedures. Avoid investigating the matter yourself; share what you know through the proper route and cooperate when asked by an authorized investigator. Raise concerns about retaliation as well, rather than assuming that a change in assignments or exclusion from meetings needs no further attention.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: If you supervise or manage. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, upright and serious, hands at his sides.
on_screen: No reassurance or repair comes first
scenes.narration: Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report protected-class allegations or incidents immediately and follow the agency's complaint and investigation procedures. The report goes to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer; DHS also directs supervisors to promptly refer these matters to Equal Opportunity and Access. Consult that division about the next steps instead of deciding that you must establish the facts before passing the concern along. Do not wait for proof, confront the person accused or try to settle the concern in a team discussion before making the required report. Explain that duty honestly so the person understands why you cannot promise to keep the matter secret or leave it unreported. Follow the authorized process and cooperate with its directions, while avoiding an inquiry of your own that could interfere with it. An apology or an effort to repair harm does not remove the duty to report or justify delaying it.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Invite before the decision closes. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand raised beside him as if holding a calendar page.
on_screen: Name what is open and who decides
Ask for the strongest case against your idea
scenes.narration: Edmondson's leadership toolkit connects how work is framed, how people are invited to contribute and what happens after someone speaks. Start by explaining the purpose of the work and where the team still faces questions that it cannot yet answer. Invite input through genuine inquiry and give colleagues a workable way to respond before the decision has already been made. A useful response values information, examines mistakes and maintains standards, rather than promising that every idea will be accepted without review. In practice, a broad request for questions at the end of a meeting may come too late to affect the work. Explain what is being decided, who decides and when people can raise a concern that will still receive a fair hearing. Asking for the strongest case against your preferred option makes the invitation more concrete; your response shows whether that challenge is welcome.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Show what changed. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, one hand open toward the points, relaxed.
on_screen: Say what changed because someone spoke up
scenes.narration: An invitation becomes credible through what colleagues can observe after someone contributes a concern, correction or alternative explanation. Explain what changed because the question was examined, or why the available evidence supported keeping the original decision or wording. This account does not need to promise agreement with every suggestion, but it should address the question that was actually raised. If a condition remains unresolved, identify the next step instead of allowing a warm acknowledgment to stand in for an answer. The reading also asks teams to examine constant urgency, because meaningful review requires time to think and a realistic way to challenge a deadline. Thank contributors in a manner that respects their preferences and the circumstances in which they shared the information. Public recognition can be welcome, but it should not expose someone who raised a concern privately or asked not to be identified.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Evidence, not a safety score. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt with his hair tied back (C7) stands full length, thoughtful, one hand at his chin.
on_screen: Do not rank people by how often they speak
scenes.narration: Changes in the number of questions or concerns can inform a review, but they cannot establish the explanation by themselves. Fewer questions might reflect clearer instructions, less opportunity to contribute or greater hesitation about the response people expect to receive. More reports might indicate an accessible route, a newly emerging problem or several conditions that need separate examination. Avoid ranking colleagues by how often they speak or assigning a label to someone whose contribution is quieter or prepared in writing. Describe which questions received substantive answers, which remain open and what the available accounts actually establish about the process. Keep an individual's description within its stated scope, and leave unreported experiences unknown rather than filling them in with assumptions. A careful account of mixed evidence gives the team a stronger basis for improvement than a single score presented as certainty.

check.prompt: You do not supervise anyone. A colleague on another team tells you a teammate keeps joking about their accommodation in front of others. They ask you to keep it between the two of you. What fits best?

options.text: Thank them, explain the limits of confidentiality and the DHS reporting expectation, and discuss the appropriate route and support they would like.

feedback.text: You took the concern seriously and explained your responsibilities without promising secrecy. DHS expects employees to promptly report these complaints to a supervisor or Equal Opportunity and Access. Support the person while following that route.
Managers and supervisors have an immediate reporting duty under Policy 1436. Explain that distinction without implying that a peer can promise to leave a complaint unreported.

options.text: Forward the account today without explaining your reporting responsibilities or discussing what support the colleague needs, assuming the formal process will address everything.

feedback.text: Reporting through the proper route is appropriate. The gap is leaving the colleague uninformed about your responsibilities and assuming that a report answers their immediate need for support.
Explain the next step before making promises. Ask about support and provide a factual account through the appropriate route without conducting your own investigation.

options.text: Talk with the teammate yourself and ask what happened, so you can tell whether the jokes were meant to hurt before anyone decides to involve Human Resources.

feedback.text: Trying to establish intent before reporting can delay the proper process and expose the colleague. Receive the account, explain your role and leave investigation to the authorized process.
What information belongs in a factual report, and what questions should the authorized investigator examine?

options.text: Agree to keep it between the two of you, since it is their experience to handle, and check in with them next week to see whether the jokes have stopped.

feedback.text: Respect for privacy matters, but an unconditional promise can conflict with reporting responsibilities. Being a peer does not remove the DHS expectation to promptly report these complaints.
Explain what you can keep private, what needs to enter the appropriate process and which support options the person can choose.

reflection: If someone brought you a concern tomorrow, would you know which routes to share? What would you need to look up first?
Which of the five Ds feels most natural to you, and which feels hardest?
When did you last hear someone say what changed because a colleague spoke up? What would it take to make that a habit?

simulations.intro: Whatever your job at DHS, you may encounter a meeting where someone raises a work question and the discussion moves on. I want you to consider that moment as a peer whose influence comes from asking, responding and following through on the work. In this scenario, you examine a shared guide, address your own error and receive a colleague’s concern without supervising anyone involved. Notice what each response makes possible and what still requires action, without assuming that one exchange determines whether someone speaks again.
simulations.title: The Monday huddle
simulations.learner_role: You are a member of a small DHS team that keeps a quick-reference guide up to date. Call-line colleagues use the guide when people ask where to send documents and whom to call. You are a peer on the team and do not supervise anyone. Your teammates include the team lead, who supervises the team and decides what goes into the guide, an experienced colleague who has worked on it for years, and a newer team member who joined six weeks ago.
simulations.background: A small DHS team holds a twenty-minute Monday huddle to review changes to the quick-reference guide that call-line colleagues use. This week’s agenda is full, and the team lead is watching the time while you prepare to discuss the contacts section you updated. The call-line lead is not attending, although her staff rely on the guide when explaining where people should send documents or seek help. The team also holds a monthly learning review, creating a later opportunity to examine errors after their immediate effects have been addressed.

decisions.setup: Halfway through the huddle, the newer team member asks why the guide directs a transfer while the training sheet says to take a message. The experienced colleague replies, “Everyone else understands it. You’re overthinking it,” and a couple of people laugh before anyone compares the instructions. The team lead starts moving to the next item, while the newer colleague looks at his notes and the work question remains unanswered.
decisions.prompt: What do you do in this moment?

choices.text: “Before we move on, can we look at that? I'm not sure how those two fit either. If they conflict, callers could get different answers. Who can confirm which one applies?”
choices.consequence: The team lead pauses while the experienced colleague compares the instructions and acknowledges that the training sheet changed last month. After asking which calls the newer member meant, the lead agrees to obtain confirmation from the person responsible and report back by Friday. The newer member writes down that commitment, leaving the answer itself pending rather than treating the question as already resolved.

feedback.text: You returned attention to the conflicting instructions and asked who could confirm the answer without deciding it yourself. Check that the promised response reaches the guide and the colleagues using it.
The newer member can now refer to a specific review commitment. That visible response matters without proving how he felt about the laughter or whether he will ask another question.
A short version works when time is tight: “Can we take thirty seconds on that? Who can confirm which one applies?”

choices.text: Say nothing now, since the huddle is short and the team lead is already moving on, and catch the newer team member afterward to walk him through how the two instructions fit together.
choices.consequence: The huddle continues to the next two items without another question, while the newer member stops writing in his notes. Nobody compares the instructions, so your intended private conversation has not yet supplied an answer or arranged a change to the guide.

feedback.text: A private conversation may help, but an intended explanation does not resolve a conflict you have not yet checked. Arrange the review needed for the shared guide rather than assuming the two instructions fit.
A stronger move keeps the question in the room for a moment and asks who can confirm the answer. Then the follow-up afterward can be about him, not about rescuing his question.
If you had asked that question and the room moved on, what would you conclude about asking the next one?

choices.text: “I think it's in last month's huddle notes. I can send you the link after this so you have it, and that way the team lead can keep the huddle on schedule.”
choices.consequence: The team lead accepts your offer to send the notes and moves on, while the newer member thanks you for the link. Neither the notes nor the two instructions have been examined during the exchange, leaving the apparent conflict available to affect the next call.

feedback.text: Pointing to a resource is helpful, but the notes may not answer whether the two instructions conflict. A stronger move asks who can confirm which applies, so the guide gets checked.
Keeping a huddle on schedule matters, and offering a link feels like a fair compromise. It does, though, quietly agree that the question was already settled.
To the call-line colleagues using both documents, the open question is not old news. It decides what they tell the next caller.

choices.text: “Good catch. The training sheet is newer, so the guide must be out of date. Let's change the guide to match it today so callers get the right instruction.”
choices.consequence: The experienced colleague points out that the newer sheet could also contain an error, and the team lead says neither instruction has been confirmed. He agrees to contact the person responsible for the training sheet before approving a change, keeping your proposed revision dependent on that check. The question now has a review route, although your initial conclusion went beyond what the two documents established.

feedback.text: You kept the question alive, which matters. The gap is that welcoming a question does not settle its answer. A stronger move asks who can confirm which one applies before anything changes.

The experienced colleague has identified another possible explanation: the training sheet could be incorrect. Examine that possibility without inferring her feelings from her posture or predicting her willingness to contribute.
Try pairing support with a check: “That's a real question. I don't know which is current. Who can confirm before we change anything?”

decisions.setup: Near the end of the agenda, the team lead asks whether anyone has another item before the huddle closes on time. The guide and training sheet have not been compared, while call-line colleagues continue using both documents to explain the next step. The newer member begins closing his laptop, but you still have an opportunity to ask how the unresolved question will be checked.
decisions.prompt: Do you say anything before the huddle ends?

choices.text: “Before we close, can we go back to the two instructions? I'm not sure they match, and callers are using both. Who could check which one callers should get?”
choices.consequence: The team lead pauses and asks which calls prompted the question, while the experienced colleague reads both instructions and acknowledges the difference. He agrees to obtain confirmation and report back by Friday, giving the unresolved issue a named next step before the huddle ends.

feedback.text: You used the last open moment to return the question to the work, and you shared the uncertainty instead of leaving it with him. Build on it by asking sooner next time, while the question is still warm.
The concern has returned to the team’s work with a commitment to seek an answer. A private check-in can offer additional support, but it serves a different purpose from resolving the instructions.

choices.text: Let the huddle close on time, then send the newer team member a friendly message: “Don't take that comment personally. You'll pick this up fast. Ask me anything, anytime, okay?”
choices.consequence: The newer member thanks you for the message, but you have not checked the instructions or arranged for anyone else to resolve the difference. Both documents remain in use, and the practical question raised in the huddle remains separate from the reassurance you offered privately.

feedback.text: A kind private message is a very common response, and it may feel good to receive. It also treats the problem as his feelings, when the problem he named is in the guide.
A stronger move brings the question back before the huddle ends, so it gets checked. The private check-in can still follow.
What would tell the newer team member that his question was useful, not just forgivable?

decisions.setup: On Tuesday, the call-line lead reports that a caller found the guide’s document-help number disconnected and asks you to check it. You recognize the number you copied from an old shared contact list last week, then find a different number on the current program page. You confirm that the program number changed months ago, while call-line staff have been supplying the old number since Thursday. Your role allows this factual correction, but the people relying on the guide also need an account of what happened.
decisions.prompt: What do you do?

choices.text: Correct the number now, tell the call-line lead and the team lead what happened, ask whether callers given the old number need follow-up, and flag the old contact list.
choices.consequence: You correct the number, and the call-line lead asks staff to identify affected contacts through their authorized records and follow-up procedure. The team lead arranges to retire the outdated list from current use under the records procedure, preserving any required history. He also asks how the obsolete source was selected, giving the next huddle a specific preparation issue to examine. The guide now contains the verified number, while the extent of earlier effects and any needed caller follow-up still require checking.

feedback.text: You handled the present need first, told the people who rely on the guide, and pointed at the condition behind the slip. Build on it by suggesting one specific change, such as checking numbers against the current program page.

The call-line lead now knows the source and can assess the affected contacts through the established process. That supports current follow-up without guaranteeing the accuracy of the rest of the guide.

choices.text: Correct the number right away, check the rest of the contacts section against the program page, and reply to the call-line lead, “Fixed, and I checked the other numbers too.”
choices.consequence: Within ten minutes, the guide contains the verified number and the remaining contact entries have been checked against current program information. The team lead has not been told about the outdated source, which remains available for another worker to use. The call-line lead knows the entry was corrected but has not received the history needed to assess follow-up for callers given the earlier number.

feedback.text: Fixing it fast and checking the rest of the section is a very natural reaction to your own slip, and both steps are right. What it leaves behind is the callers who already have the old number, and the list that caused it.
A stronger move adds two sentences: what happened, and where the old number came from. That turns a private fix into something the team can learn from.
If a teammate had made this slip, what would you want them to tell the team?

choices.text: Correct the number, then post a long apology in the team chat saying you feel terrible, should have checked, and promise it will never happen again because you will triple-check everything.
choices.consequence: Two teammates reply to your apology with reassurance, and the experienced colleague adds a heart reaction after you correct the number. The call-line lead is outside that chat and has not received an explanation of the source or the possible need for caller follow-up. The obsolete list remains available, so the promise to avoid all future mistakes has not changed the source-checking step.

feedback.text: Owning the mistake matters, and you did. The gap is that the apology goes to the team chat, while the call-line lead and the callers still need something specific. A plain account to them would do more.
Feeling terrible about a mistake is human. A promise never to slip again offers a certainty nobody can deliver; one changed step, like checking the program page, can actually be tested.
Try: “I copied the old number from an outdated list. It's fixed. Here's who may need a callback, and here's the list to retire.”

choices.text: Add the error to the team's monthly learning review next week, so the cause gets examined properly with everyone instead of patched in a rush today.
choices.consequence: You add the issue to next week’s learning agenda without correcting the guide or answering the call-line lead’s immediate question. The disconnected number remains available to staff assisting callers, while the planned review has not addressed the current information gap.

feedback.text: Wanting the cause examined properly is a good learning instinct. The timing is the problem: callers are being given a disconnected number today, and a meeting next week cannot fix that.
A stronger move corrects the guide and answers the call-line lead now, then brings the how-it-happened question to the review.

decisions.setup: Twenty minutes later, the call-line lead writes again and copies the team lead, asking where the outdated number came from. She notes that some callers may still be trying it and asks whether the same source was used elsewhere in the guide. Your earlier response has not yet addressed the possible follow-up for callers or explained how the old contact list influenced the update.
decisions.prompt: How do you reply?

choices.text: “That's on me: I copied it from an old contact list. I'll make sure the guide is correct now and check other sections. Could your staff note callers who mention it?”
choices.consequence: You explain the source and complete the checks, while the team lead arranges to retire the old list from current use under the records procedure. The call-line lead asks staff to identify affected callers through the authorized follow-up process rather than creating a separate informal contact list. Within the hour, the guide is corrected and the team has a specific source-checking question for the next huddle. Any remaining caller effects still need follow-through; identifying the problem does not establish that everyone who received the number has been reached.

feedback.text: You gave a plain account, fixed the present problem and asked for what callers need. Build on it next time by saying all of that in your first reply.
Knowing the source helps the call-line lead assess the scope of the problem, but other entries still need their own checks. One explanation cannot establish that the entire guide is reliable.

choices.text: “It's a small thing, and I'll make sure it's right. Callers can always find the current number on the program page, so I really don't think anyone else needs to get involved here.”
choices.consequence: The call-line lead does not reply, and the team lead contacts you privately to ask again where the number came from. People who wrote down the old number still have it, and the obsolete list remains available to anyone updating the guide. Your assurance has not answered whether the problem appears elsewhere or supplied the information needed to assess affected contacts.
