feedback.text: Keeping a slip in proportion is reasonable, but this reply answers neither of her questions. A stronger move says where the number came from and whether it could be elsewhere.
For a caller waiting on help that is not coming, the program page is not much use if they never think to look. The call-line lead is speaking for them.
What makes a mistake feel smaller when you describe it, and who carries the difference?

decisions.setup: Later on Tuesday, the newer team member asks to speak in a small meeting room about a colleague from another team. He reports repeated use of an unwanted shortened name despite requests to stop, followed by a comment that his name is too difficult. He says the colleague repeated it after the huddle in front of call-line staff, some of whom laughed during the exchange. He is unsure how to raise the concern and worries about making it a larger issue between the teams.
decisions.prompt: What do you say?

choices.text: “Thank you for telling me. That needs attention. Before I promise privacy, let me explain our reporting responsibilities and the support you can choose. What would help right now?”
choices.consequence: He says he is worried about what happens next. You explain that DHS expects employees to promptly report discrimination, harassment or retaliation complaints to a supervisor or Equal Opportunity and Access. The appropriate agency staff determine how the concern is classified; he does not need to prove a violation first. You also explain that the team lead has an immediate reporting duty as a supervisor. You discuss the appropriate route together and offer company while following the reporting expectation. He asks about support from his union representative, and you help him locate the contact. You do not promise an outcome or confront the other colleague.

feedback.text: You took the concern seriously, explained your responsibilities and preserved choices about support without promising secrecy. Follow through on the reporting route and check what support would help next.
His concern about what happens next deserves a clear explanation. Knowing the limits at the start is more dependable than learning later that a promise could not be kept.
If you witness the behavior, a safe interruption and a later check-in can support him. Those actions accompany reporting duties rather than replace them.

choices.text: “I will tell the team lead today. Once I send it, there is nothing else we need to discuss; he will handle everything.”
choices.consequence: He asks what the team lead will do and whether the other colleague will know. You have not explained the reporting process or its limits, and you cannot promise how it will unfold. Telling the appropriate person is a valid step, but your assurance that everything will be handled leaves his questions and immediate need for support unanswered.

feedback.text: The problem is not reporting through an appropriate route. It is promising a result and closing the conversation before explaining your responsibilities or hearing what support he needs.
Explain the reporting expectation, distinguish what you know from what the agency process will determine, and ask about support without delaying the required next step.
Which parts of the next step can you explain accurately, and which outcomes are outside your control?

choices.text: “That's not okay. I know him a little. I'll find him tomorrow, ask what he was thinking, and tell him to use your full name. He'll listen to me.”
choices.consequence: He asks you not to approach the colleague, explaining that he fears wider disclosure and further difficulty between the teams. He then says he will handle it himself and leaves before you explain the reporting process, its limits or available support. Your proposed confrontation has not addressed the responsibilities that apply to the concern he described.

feedback.text: Confronting the colleague yourself can expose the person who spoke to you and interfere with the proper process. Explain your reporting role rather than investigating or promising an informal resolution.
A peer confronting the other colleague may create the exposure he fears without giving him an accurate account of the agency process.
A useful opening is: “Here is what I need to report and where it goes. What support would help you while that happens?”

choices.text: “I'm sure he doesn't mean anything by it. He jokes with everyone. Maybe just laugh it off, or ask him again in a friendly way so it doesn't get awkward between teams.”
choices.consequence: He nods and ends the conversation without discussing the reporting route or support, and you do not raise those points before he leaves. In the scenario’s next meeting, the colleague repeats the unwanted name and nobody responds during the exchange. That observed silence does not establish what participants thought, but the reported behavior and your reporting responsibility remain unaddressed.

feedback.text: The reported behavior continued after he asked for it to stop, and reassurance about intent does not resolve that account. Explain the reporting responsibilities and support options without requiring him to prove a violation first.

An explanation based on presumed good intentions supplies a motive the colleague has not established. Respond to the reported behavior and its context while leaving any finding to the authorized process.
What did he need to hear to know it was okay to take this further?

practiced: Bringing a dismissed question back to the work without making the person who asked it the topic
Admitting your own uncertainty so others can look again
Handling your own mistake in the present before turning it into a lesson
Giving a plain account of what happened and where it came from
Explaining reporting responsibilities while respecting a colleague's privacy and choices about support
Knowing that a supervisor must report a protected-class concern right away, and saying so honestly
this_week: In your next meeting, if a question gets brushed aside, try one sentence that brings it back: “Who can confirm which one applies?”
When you find an error, address the immediate work need and tell the people who rely on it what happened. Then examine the cause and any follow-up still required.
Look up the current contacts for Human Resources, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division and the Employee Assistance Program, so you can share them if someone asks.
When someone questions your work this week, ask one clarifying question before you explain.

simulations.intro: If you work a front desk, a phone line or a schedule, you may notice a process problem before it reaches the people responsible for changing it. I have found it easy to fix a problem quietly and move on. Here, you respond to a missing interpreter with a visitor waiting, raise a template problem in a rushed huddle, and decide how to address a comment about a colleague.
simulations.title: The Rescheduled Appointment
simulations.learner_role: You are an Office and Administrative Specialist at a DHS front desk. You greet visitors, schedule appointments, and arrange interpreters and accommodations through the scheduling system. You are not a supervisor. Changes to the shared scheduling template, and anything a policy requires, belong to your supervisor or the person or area responsible.
simulations.background: A visitor arrives for a ten o’clock appointment that you booked two weeks ago, when he requested an interpreter and you entered the request. Last week your teammate moved the appointment to today, but no interpreter is booked in the current record for the meeting. Reviewing the record, you discover that the team’s template clears the interpreter request field when an appointment is rescheduled. The visitor waits in the lobby holding his appointment letter, while you consider how to address the immediate need and examine the process. In this example, the local practice is to offer a telephone interpreter now or a new appointment, according to the visitor’s preference.

decisions.setup: Your teammate returns from break and notices the record on your screen, asking, “Oh no. Did I do that?” The visitor watches from the lobby and holds up his appointment letter, pointing to the line that confirms an interpreter was requested. You need to address the visitor’s immediate options while deciding how to discuss the record with your teammate.
decisions.prompt: What do you do first?

choices.text: Get a phone interpreter on the line and ask the visitor whether to go ahead now or rebook. Then show your teammate how the request field cleared when the date moved.
choices.consequence: With a telephone interpreter available, the visitor chooses to continue and the appointment starts twenty minutes later than scheduled. Your teammate studies the record and asks, “So it wasn’t just me?” You explain, “The template cleared it. Neither of us thought to re-check it, either.” He notes the case through the authorized record system so he can examine other appointments he rescheduled.

feedback.text: You took care of the person waiting before the conversation about how it happened, and you let him choose. Then you showed your teammate the record instead of a verdict. Build on it: the template issue you just found affects more than one appointment, so it needs to reach the person who can change it.

Showing the record gives your teammate a specific process to examine alongside the missed check. His decision to review other appointments is observable; whether he feels safer raising a future mistake remains his to describe.

choices.text: Book the phone interpreter for the visitor, fix the record yourself, and tell your teammate not to worry about it, since everyone misses things and he looks upset enough already.
choices.consequence: You begin calling the telephone interpreter, and your teammate returns to his queue without seeing how the request disappeared from the record. The visitor remains at the counter without being asked whether he prefers to continue with that interpreter or arrange another appointment.

feedback.text: Reassuring an upset colleague is kind, and fixing it fast is a strength at a front desk. But reassurance without the record leaves the actual problem where it was, and the visitor’s choice was made for him.
Compare “don’t worry about it” with “look, the field cleared when the date moved.” Both are kind. Only one helps him, and the next person, avoid it.

choices.text: Ask your teammate, right there at the desk, why he did not check the interpreter field when he moved the appointment, so the visitor can see the problem is being taken seriously.
choices.consequence: Your teammate’s face reddens as he begins explaining what happened on the day he moved the appointment in the scheduling system. The visitor waits through the exchange without being asked which of the available options would work for him today.

feedback.text: The visitor waits while staff discuss the error, without knowing what choices are available for the appointment. Your teammate must answer a question about his actions in public, which may make a useful review harder.
The question “why didn’t you check?” assumes the cause. The record could have answered it in seconds: the template cleared the field.
When a mistake surfaces in front of the public, take care of the person first, then look at the record together, privately.

choices.text: Tell the visitor there is no interpreter today and rebook him for next week with the request entered again, so the appointment can be done properly the first time around.
choices.consequence: The visitor looks between the letter and you before explaining that he traveled by bus and took the morning off work. Your teammate remains silent, and the visitor has not agreed to a new appointment or been offered the telephone interpreter available in this example.

feedback.text: Rebooking may be what he wants, but you decided it for him. This office’s own practice offers him a choice. Ask before you arrange.
When something goes wrong for a visitor, how often is the fix you offer the one that is easiest for the office?

decisions.setup: Yesterday afternoon, you tested the template on two practice records and confirmed that rescheduling cleared the interpreter field in both cases. At this morning’s huddle, your supervisor moves quickly through the schedule because three staff members are absent and a full lobby is expected. She asks, “Any questions? No? Good,” and begins to stand before you have raised the finding, while your teammate sits beside you.
decisions.prompt: What do you do?

choices.text: Say, “One thing before you go: rescheduling clears the interpreter field. It happened yesterday and on two test records.” Ask who can fix the template, and what to do until then.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor sits down again to examine the practice records and asks how you identified the problem with the template. She agrees to send the finding to the person or area responsible for the scheduling system that day. Until a repair is confirmed, she asks everyone to check the interpreter field after rescheduling and thanks you for raising the issue. Your teammate adds that he had not known the field cleared when an appointment moved, making that information explicit to the team.

feedback.text: You gave the supervisor a concise finding supported by practice records, then asked about a repair and an interim check. Once the template changes, test a practice reschedule and share the result so the team knows what has been verified.

The supervisor’s rushed invitation provided little time for a response, whatever she intended. Your specific question gave her an opportunity to reconsider the agenda and address a problem affecting today’s appointments.
What made the test records worth the extra ten minutes yesterday?

choices.text: Let the huddle end and email your supervisor a clear write-up with the records attached. She is under real pressure this morning, and an email lets her read it when she can.
choices.consequence: The huddle ends and your supervisor begins another call before discussing a temporary response to the scheduling problem with the team. Your teammate asks, “Shouldn’t we have said something?” Two reschedules already appear on today’s list, although no shared checking instruction has been agreed.

feedback.text: A written account can be useful when a supervisor is busy, but its timing matters when appointments are already being rescheduled. A brief alert can establish the immediate need while the detailed account follows.

The written evidence supports the repair request, while a timely conversation gives the supervisor a chance to agree on an interim check. Mentioning the issue alone does not guarantee that a shared instruction follows.

choices.text: Say yesterday’s visitor had no interpreter because an appointment was moved without checking the request, and remind everyone to check the field whenever they reschedule anything.
choices.consequence: Team members know who moved yesterday’s appointment, and your teammate looks down while the reminder is discussed in the huddle. Your supervisor responds, “Good reminder,” and stands, without hearing the test results or identifying who should address the template itself.

feedback.text: A reminder is a reasonable step, but it framed the problem as a person forgetting, when you had tested the template and found the cause. Compare: “Rescheduling clears the field, on any appointment.”
From your teammate’s seat, this was his mistake described to the whole team, with the part that would have explained it left out.

choices.text: Say nothing at the huddle. Your supervisor is short three people, the template is not yours, and your teammate might feel exposed if the visitor story comes up in front of everyone.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor ends the huddle without hearing the finding, and the template continues clearing the interpreter field when appointments move. Other team members have not received the information needed to recognize that behavior or agree on a temporary check.

feedback.text: Protecting a teammate is a good reason to be careful. But you could raise the template without the story: it is a process problem, not a person problem.
Lead with the process: “Rescheduling clears the interpreter field. Can we check it after every reschedule until it’s fixed?”

decisions.setup: Later that week, a coworker comments in the break room, “He’s always rushing. No wonder that interpreter fell through.” Your teammate stands at the microwave with his back turned, while two others look toward you because you were at the desk that morning. You have information about the scheduling template that is missing from the explanation the coworker has just offered.
decisions.prompt: What do you say?

choices.text: Say, evenly, that you saw the record: the template clears the field when a date moves, and it would have caught any of you. Later, check in with your teammate.
choices.consequence: The coworker replies, “Huh. I didn’t know that,” and someone asks what will happen with the template now that the problem is known. During the later private conversation, your teammate says the comment bothered him and asks to see the practice records to inform his own checks. You discuss his request without repeating other people’s remarks or deciding how he should feel about what happened.

feedback.text: You supplied relevant evidence without adding another personal judgment, then asked your teammate privately about his experience. That conversation gives him room to express preferences, while any reporting responsibilities that apply still remain in effect.
The coworker acknowledged that she had not known about the template. That response shows the information was new to her; it does not establish a lasting change in her view of your teammate.

choices.text: Lighten it with a joke about how everyone rushes in a short-staffed week, and change the subject, so your teammate is not embarrassed in front of the whole room.
choices.consequence: People laugh and the conversation moves on, while your teammate leaves the room carrying his lunch without discussing the comment. No one hears the information about the template, leaving the claim about rushing unanswered by the available evidence.

feedback.text: Distraction can interrupt a difficult moment, but here the evidence about the template remained absent from the conversation. A brief factual correction would add information without requiring a judgment about the coworker’s motives.
After a joke moves a room on, what story do people leave with?

choices.text: Tell the coworker, in front of everyone, that talking about a colleague behind his back is unprofessional, and that she should keep comments like that to herself from now on.
choices.consequence: The room becomes quiet, and the coworker says she was only joking before leaving without discussing the template problem. Your teammate has heard the exchange, but the information explaining how the interpreter request disappeared still has not been shared.

feedback.text: You were right that the comment was unfair. But a public rebuke made the moment about her conduct, not about what happened. Naming behavior directly works best when it is likely to help rather than escalate.
From your teammate’s side, being defended loudly can be almost as exposing as being criticized.
A fact can do the work of a rebuke: “Actually, the template clears the field when a date moves. It would have caught any of us.”

choices.text: Say nothing in the room, and mention the comment to your supervisor at your one-to-one next week, since correcting a coworker in front of others could make things awkward for everyone there.
choices.consequence: Two people nod without hearing the information about the template, and subsequent retellings continue to describe the incident as rushing. By the time you raise the comment with your supervisor, your teammate is checking every entry silently and asking fewer questions. Those observations warrant a conversation about support; they do not establish what your teammate thinks or why his participation has changed.

feedback.text: Staying out of break-room talk is a common way to avoid conflict, and telling your supervisor is a real route. But you held the one fact that changed the story, and a week is long enough for a label to set. A label that sticks can narrow how a colleague is seen, while the real cause goes unfixed.
If the comment had been about you, what would you have wanted the person who saw the record to say?

decisions.setup: The visitor remains at the counter beside your teammate, without having been asked which available option he prefers for his appointment. Your teammate also has not seen the evidence that rescheduling cleared the interpreter field, leaving both the immediate choice and the process discussion unresolved.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: With a phone interpreter on the line, ask the visitor whether to go ahead now or rebook with one in person. Then show your teammate how the field cleared.
choices.consequence: The visitor chooses to proceed with the telephone interpreter, after which your teammate reviews the record and says, “So the move cleared it.” He identifies the case through the authorized record system so he can check other appointments he has rescheduled.

feedback.text: You put the visitor’s choice first and then gave your teammate the facts instead of a verdict. Build on it: ask the person affected before you arrange the fix, every time.
For the visitor, being asked turned a mistake about him into a decision he made himself.

choices.text: Apologize to the visitor for the mix-up, offer him a phone interpreter, and tell your teammate you will talk about the record later, once the lobby is quiet.
choices.consequence: The visitor accepts the offered telephone interpreter, allowing the appointment to proceed while you defer the discussion with your teammate. Because the lobby remains busy and no time was agreed, that conversation does not take place during the day.

feedback.text: The apology and offer helped the visitor. Offering one option is better than none, but asking which he preferred would have been better still. Showing the record later is fine, if later actually comes.
If you defer a conversation, set a time: “Can we look at this at two?”

choices.text: Let your teammate take it from here, since he moved the appointment, and go back to the phone queue that has been building up while all of this was happening.
choices.consequence: Your teammate books a telephone interpreter without first asking the visitor which option he prefers for the appointment. The record remains unchanged, and your teammate has not received the explanation you found about how rescheduling cleared the field.

feedback.text: A building queue pulls everyone back to the phones. But you held the explanation, and handing over the visitor without it left your teammate to guess.
What would it have cost to spend one more minute at the counter?

decisions.setup: The huddle has ended without an agreed response to the template issue, and today’s appointment list already includes several reschedules. Your supervisor is heading to another call, leaving a brief opportunity to raise the finding before the team begins that work.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: Catch your supervisor before her call: “Thirty seconds. Rescheduling clears the interpreter field; I tested it twice. Who can fix the template, and what should the team do today?”
choices.consequence: Your supervisor pauses to review the finding and agrees to send it to the person or area responsible for the scheduling system. She asks you to tell the team to check the interpreter field after every reschedule until the problem is fixed. Before leaving, she adds, “Next time, say it in the huddle. That’s what it’s for,” giving you an explicit invitation to raise similar findings.

feedback.text: You caught the moment before it was gone, with something short and specific. Build on her answer: she has just told you the huddle is a place for this. Use it next time.
From your supervisor’s side, a thirty-second heads-up is far easier than finding out after a second visitor waits without an interpreter.

choices.text: Tell the two teammates sitting next to you to re-check the interpreter field on every reschedule today, and plan to raise the template at tomorrow’s huddle instead.
choices.consequence: The two teammates you tell begin checking their reschedules, but the rest of the team has not received that information. Discussion of the template and a shared response remains deferred until tomorrow, despite the appointments being changed today.

feedback.text: The nearby teammates now have a useful check, but others still lack the information and the shared template remains unchanged. Raise the finding with your supervisor or the person or area responsible so a wider response can be considered.
When you find a shared problem, tell the people near you and the person who can fix it.

choices.text: Wait for a calmer day to raise it. Your supervisor has enough on her plate this morning, and one missed interpreter does not make the template an emergency for anyone.
choices.consequence: The team remains busy through the following day without discussing the finding or agreeing on an interim checking process. Each reschedule still clears the interpreter field, so the same problem remains available to affect another appointment.

feedback.text: Waiting for a quieter moment is understandable, but the problem can continue affecting appointments while the team remains busy. A concise alert about the tested behavior helps separate the immediate need from the longer repair discussion.
How many reschedules happen on your team in a week, and how many would it take to make this urgent?

practiced: Taking care of the person affected first, and asking what they want before arranging a fix
Showing a colleague the record instead of a verdict after a mistake
Raising a tested process problem briefly in a rushed meeting, with a request for a fix and a rule for today
Separating a process gap from a person’s error
Answering a personal label with a plain fact, without shaming anyone
Checking in privately with a colleague after a comment about him
this_week: Choose one scheduling or intake step where information might be lost. Use an authorized practice record to test it, and share a confirmed problem with your supervisor.
At your next huddle, if something affects today’s work, say it in one sentence before the meeting ends.
If you hear a colleague described by a label after a mistake, add one fact about what actually happened.

simulations.intro: If you build tables, dashboards or evaluations, your work is trusted because people assume someone checked it. I know the feeling of finding my own error after a number has already left my desk. Here, you decide what to do with that error, how to help a team learn from it without blame or excuses, and what to say when someone asks you to put a number on how safe people feel.
simulations.title: The Number in the Briefing
simulations.learner_role: You are a Management Analyst on a research and evaluation team. You build tables and dashboards that program staff and leaders rely on. You own the accuracy of your own analysis. What a program does with a result, and any formal performance matter, belong to the person or area responsible.
simulations.background: Last week, you sent a DHS program director a table of application processing times, with results grouped by region and recorded language preference. One comparison used the average for applicants selecting a language other than English against the average for all applications, including those with an unknown language preference. The director quoted that comparison in a leadership briefing as evidence that the processing-time gap had closed during the reporting period. While preparing the next quarterly analysis, you discover that a join excluded cases with blank language fields from the overall comparison group. Restoring those cases changes the overall average: the gap has narrowed, but it has not closed, and blank preferences remain classified as unknown. A peer reviewed the query before release, but you wrote the code and remain responsible for explaining the correction.

decisions.setup: The peer analyst reviews the error and says, “The briefing’s done. Fix it in next quarter’s table and add a footnote. Nobody reads footnotes, and nobody needs to know it was us.” Your research manager is across the room, and the director has another leadership briefing in two weeks where the original figure could be repeated.
decisions.prompt: What do you do with the error?

choices.text: Tell your research manager today: the figure the director quoted, the corrected figure, and how the join dropped blank-language cases. Then ask her how the correction should reach the director.
choices.consequence: Your manager asks about the join and thanks you for raising the correction before the director’s next scheduled briefing. She requests a note showing both figures and agrees to call the director with you that afternoon, while the peer analyst offers to help prepare the explanation.

feedback.text: You raised your own error while it could still change something, and you brought specifics instead of an apology. Asking how the correction should reach the director left that decision with the person who owns the relationship. Build on it: put the old and new figures side by side in the note, so nobody has to work out what changed.
From the director’s side, hearing it now, with a corrected figure in hand, is very different from discovering it in a footnote after repeating the old number.

choices.text: Correct the query and send the director a revised table yourself today, marked revised in a footnote, so he has the right number before his next briefing.
choices.consequence: While drafting the revised table, you notice that the footnote labels it revised without identifying the changed figure or its use in the earlier briefing. The email has not been sent, so there is still time to make the correction and its practical implications explicit.

feedback.text: Getting the right number to the director is the heart of it, and you moved fast. The gap is in how it lands. A footnote that says “revised” hides the part he most needs: his briefing used a figure that no longer holds.
When a result has already been used, say so plainly: “The figure you quoted on the language gap was too low because of a join error. Here is the corrected figure.”

choices.text: Before telling anyone, rerun every table you have sent out this year to see whether the join affected others too, so you can report the full scope in one clean message.
choices.consequence: By late afternoon, you have checked four tables without identifying another error, while the director still holds the incorrect figure. When your manager asks how the quarterly rerun is progressing, you answer, “Fine,” without explaining the correction already confirmed.

feedback.text: Checking the scope is useful, but it need not postpone disclosure of an error already confirmed in a figure being used. Explain what is known now and identify the additional checks still underway.
When you hold an error until it feels complete, whose discomfort is the waiting protecting?

choices.text: Go with the peer analyst’s plan. The corrected figure will be in next quarter’s table, the change is smaller than it looks, and naming it now could embarrass the director.
choices.consequence: You add a footnote to the next quarterly draft without alerting the director to the incorrect figure in the previous briefing. An email then arrives requesting reuse of the same slide at a county-partner meeting, making another possible use of the error explicit.

feedback.text: From the director’s seat, protecting him from embarrassment now means he repeats the old figure to more people. The kindness lands on the wrong side of the error.
Going along with a trusted colleague’s plan is a very human move, especially when the plan spares you both. Shame can hide useful information, and quiet fixes can leave the actual problem in place.
If a colleague suggests keeping it quiet, try: “I’d rather tell our manager today. Will you look at the note with me?”

decisions.setup: By the end of the week, your manager and the director know about the error, and the director has corrected the briefing note. During a thirty-minute review, your manager says, “I want to learn from this, not hang it on anyone.” The peer analyst attributes the error entirely to the template’s join, while another analyst says the code author should have identified it. As colleagues look toward you, consider how the template, review process and your own choices contributed to the result.
decisions.prompt: What do you contribute to the review?

choices.text: Say the template’s join and your own choice to skip a row-count check both played a part. Propose a row-count check before any table leaves the team, and ask who owns it.
choices.consequence: The peer analyst explains that his review checklist did not require a row-count comparison, adding another condition for the team to examine. Your manager records the proposed check, assigns responsibility, and schedules a review after the next two releases to assess its use and results. The discussion identifies a concrete responsibility and process change without dismissing the error or labeling you careless.

feedback.text: You held both explanations at once: the template made the error easy, and your choice let it through. That is learning with accountability. Then you made it testable, with one specific check and an owner. Build on it by reviewing whether the check is actually used.

The peer analyst added information about his checklist after you described your own missed check. That exchange provides evidence for the review without establishing how either person felt or guaranteeing future disclosure.

choices.text: Say the error was yours alone and the template is fine. Promise to double-check every table yourself, starting with next quarter’s release, so it cannot happen again.
choices.consequence: Your manager acknowledges your willingness to take responsibility and moves toward closing the review without changing the template or shared checking process. The promise to check everything depends on one person, while another analyst using the same template would still encounter its exclusion of blank-language cases.

feedback.text: Owning your part was right in spirit. But taking all of it erased a condition the team could change. A promise never to make a mistake again changes nothing specific; a changed task is more useful than a vow.
When you take all the blame in a review, what part of the process do you leave unexamined?

choices.text: Agree with the peer analyst that the template caused it, so the review stays blame-free and people feel safe naming errors without anyone being held responsible for them.
choices.consequence: The discussion moves away from individual blame without assigning responsibility for a change to the template or the review procedure. Your manager notes that she still needs to explain what action will address the problem before another release reaches the director.

feedback.text: A blame-free review sounds like psychological safety, and the wish behind it is good. The line is clear: a template gap matters, but it does not mean nobody had a responsibility. Removing every role from the story leaves the next task without an owner.

Compare “the system did it” with “the template drops blank fields, and the review did not check row counts.” The second identifies conditions and responsibilities that the team can examine without assigning a character label.

choices.text: Let your manager and the peer analyst work it out. You already admitted the error once, and saying more about your own part might sound defensive or turn the review back on you.
choices.consequence: Colleagues continue debating whether the template or the code author caused the error, without hearing your account of the checks you skipped. The discussion settles on a general reminder to be careful, leaving the specific join behavior and checking process unchanged.

feedback.text: Your silence left your colleagues to argue about your work without the one person who knew how it happened. To them, it may have looked like you agreed with whichever version won.
In a review of your own error, one plain sentence is enough: “Here is what the template did, and here is what I did. I would suggest this one change.”

decisions.setup: A month later, your manager forwards a director’s request for an individual speaking-up score based on how often each employee talks in team meetings. The director also wants the report to describe the division as psychologically safe because no complaints were received during the previous quarter. Your manager asks whether you can scope the work by Friday, giving you an opportunity to examine what the proposed measures could establish.
decisions.prompt: How do you respond to the request?

choices.text: Propose tracking whether questions and errors reached a decision and got an answer, report it with its limits, and explain why speaking counts and zero complaints cannot show safety.
choices.consequence: Your note proposes tracing a small set of questions and errors through to the response, describing what those examples can and cannot establish. It explains that complaint counts can reflect several conditions, including reporting opportunities and willingness to report, rather than proving a particular climate. Any proposed climate survey is referred to the person or area responsible for its design, privacy and interpretation. The director drops the individual score, and the report instead describes the reviewed examples and the questions that remain unanswered.

feedback.text: You kept the director’s real goal, knowing whether people can raise problems, and offered evidence that fits it. You also kept people from being ranked by airtime. Build on it: the briefing correction is itself a pathway worth following, from raised error to changed decision.
Think of the analyst who writes careful review notes but rarely speaks in meetings. Under a speaking count, that person looks disengaged. Under your proposal, their contributions count.
When you report process evidence, add one sentence on its limits every time. It keeps the next reader from turning a pathway into a safety rating.

choices.text: Build the score by Friday but report only team averages, so nobody is ranked by name, and keep the safety line, since a quarter with no complaints is some evidence.
choices.consequence: The report uses team averages, with lower results for teams that communicate mainly in writing and hold fewer meetings. It also retains the unsupported statement about psychological safety, while two analysts later report that their team’s score was discussed in individual supervision meetings.

feedback.text: Removing names was a real protection. But the measure still counts speaking turns, which rewards one visible style, and the safety line still treats silence as proof. The stronger choice changes what is measured, not just who is named.
What else could explain a quarter with no complaints, besides people feeling safe?

choices.text: Tell your manager the request is a bad idea and you will not build it, because psychological safety cannot be measured and the director should know better than to ask.
choices.consequence: Your manager asks for an explanation she can take to the director, then assigns the request to another analyst who builds the proposed score. The report includes the measure without your concerns or a description of a more suitable way to examine the director’s question.

feedback.text: The proposed speaking count does not establish psychological safety, but that does not mean the concept cannot be studied. Explain the measurement problem and propose an appropriate review of process evidence or a carefully designed team-level survey.
From your manager’s side, she now has to manage both the director’s request and your refusal, with no alternative to offer him.

choices.text: Build it as asked. The director owns the report, and raising doubts about a director’s idea right after your own error might not land well.
choices.consequence: The published score places two analysts with detailed written review notes among the lowest-ranked employees because their contributions were not spoken in meetings. The report describes the division as psychologically safe without establishing how raised questions were received or whether they informed decisions.

feedback.text: After your own error, hesitating to question a director is understandable. Notice that this is the same interpersonal risk the score claims to measure, and it kept useful knowledge out of the report.
Questioning a request can be framed as helping it succeed: “Here is a version that would tell you whether questions reach decisions.”

decisions.setup: It is still the day you discovered the error, and both you and the peer analyst have seen the corrected figure. Your manager has not been informed, while the director retains the original number for use in subsequent briefings and discussions.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: Walk over to your research manager and say, “I found an error in the table the director quoted. Here is what changed. How should he hear about it?”
choices.consequence: Your manager asks about the join, thanks you for raising the issue that day and requests a note showing the original and corrected figures. She agrees to call the director with you that afternoon so the correction can be explained alongside its implications for the briefing.

feedback.text: You raised the confirmed error while the director could still correct its use. Further scope checks can continue alongside that notification; neither a polished message nor a completed review of every table is required to explain the known problem.
What made the walk across the room feel easier now than it did this morning?

choices.text: Email the director directly with the corrected table and a plain explanation of the error, and copy your research manager so she sees it at the same moment he does.
choices.consequence: The director thanks you for the correction but asks how it should be reflected in the leadership briefing already delivered. Your manager says she would have preferred to discuss the correction first, while acknowledging that it was important to raise it that day.

feedback.text: The correction was explicit and timely, while consulting your manager first could have helped coordinate the briefing response in this scenario. Follow the reporting and correction procedures that apply to the work rather than treating one communication route as universal.
Your manager learned about her team’s error from her own inbox, at the same time as the director. She can support you better when she is not surprised.

choices.text: Go with the peer analyst’s footnote plan, but note in the team’s review log that the peer review missed the join, so the record is clear.
choices.consequence: The log identifies the missed peer review without explaining your coding decision, while the director continues to hold the incorrect figure. After reading the entry, the peer analyst stops responding to messages, and your manager asks to discuss it the following morning.

feedback.text: A record of what happened can help learning, but this one moved the error onto someone else while the director still had the old number. The present problem comes first; the account of how it happened comes after.

The record names the reviewer’s omission without your own coding decision, leaving an incomplete account of how the result was produced. Include relevant actions and conditions without assuming how the reviewer will respond to future requests.

decisions.setup: Before closing the review, your manager asks whether anyone has anything else to add, leaving time to propose a specific next step. The template’s join and the process for checking tables remain unchanged, regardless of how responsibility has been described during the discussion.
decisions.prompt: What do you say?

choices.text: Say one fix is worth leaving with: a row-count check before and after the join. Offer to draft it this week, and ask who will review it.
choices.consequence: Your manager accepts the proposal and names the peer analyst to review the check you will draft during the coming week. The review closes with responsibility assigned for a specific change and a plan to examine its use after the next release.

feedback.text: You used the last ten minutes to turn a hard conversation into one specific change. Offering to draft it kept your own responsibility visible without making it a confession. Build on it by checking, after the next release, whether the row count caught anything.
The manager can now describe an assigned action and its planned review to the director, instead of relying on a general assurance that everyone will be more careful.

choices.text: Suggest a refresher training on joins for all analysts next month, so everyone’s skills are current before the next quarterly release.
choices.consequence: Your manager records the proposed refresher, but no interim check or template revision is assigned before the next working day. Additional instruction may help analysts, while the existing join can continue excluding blank-language cases from the overall comparison.

feedback.text: Training is a reasonable idea. But it treats the gap as skill alone, when the template and the review checklist also played a part. A specific change to the work catches what a refresher can miss.
Pair any training idea with one change to the work itself: “And until then, a row-count check before release.”

choices.text: Say nothing else. The review has been uncomfortable enough, and closing it now lets everyone get back to the quarterly release on time without more back and forth.
choices.consequence: The review ends without a specific change to the template or the checks required before a table is released. A subsequent analysis using the unchanged join would exclude the same category of records unless someone identifies and corrects it.

feedback.text: Wanting an uncomfortable meeting to end is natural. Avoiding an error because the discussion feels uncomfortable leaves the problem and its conditions unchanged.
What is one change you could have proposed in a single sentence?

practiced: Raising your own error while it can still change a decision, with the old and new figures side by side
Choosing a route for a correction that leaves the relationship decision with the person who owns it
Naming both the condition and your own choice in a review, without blame or a blanket excuse
Turning a lesson into one specific, owned and testable change
Offering process evidence in place of a speaking count or a no-complaints claim
Saying plainly what a measure cannot show
this_week: Add one row-count or record-count check to a table or dashboard you send out, and note what it would have caught.
If you confirm an error in a result already used, promptly alert the person or area responsible under your team’s correction procedure. Show the original and corrected figures.
Read one report line that claims something about how staff feel, and ask what evidence it rests on and what it cannot show.

simulations.intro: If you work an eligibility line or renewal queue, you rely on shared tools such as desk aids, templates and colleagues’ explanations. I have found that questioning a familiar tool can feel difficult when an experienced worker created it and others use it daily. Here, you notice a possible gap in a DHS renewal desk aid and decide how to raise it, support a newer colleague and examine your own cases.
simulations.title: The Desk Aid
simulations.learner_role: You process health care renewals and take calls on an eligibility line. You are not the lead worker or a supervisor. You can ask questions, flag a gap and correct your own work through the team’s process. How a policy applies to a case belongs to the person or area responsible for policy interpretation.
simulations.background: Your DHS eligibility team uses a one-page renewal desk aid that the lead worker prepared two years ago and colleagues consult daily. This morning, a caller asked why her renewal letter requested different income proof from what a worker described during an earlier call. Comparing the desk aid with the current manual, you find different wording but have not established which conditions apply to her case. The lead worker will run the morning huddle in five minutes, with your supervisor expected to attend the opening discussion. The renewal conditions and case outcomes are fictional; actual questions about requirements, deadlines and corrections follow the current program procedure.

decisions.setup: Twelve people have joined the huddle when the lead worker reviews the queue and asks, “Anything on renewals before we start?” Your supervisor is present, and the newer worker who joined last month has her microphone muted while listening to the discussion. You have the desk aid and manual open side by side, but still need confirmation about which condition applies to the caller.
decisions.prompt: What do you say?

choices.text: Say the desk aid’s income-proof line reads differently from the current manual page, that a caller noticed this morning, that you may be missing a condition, and ask who can confirm.
choices.consequence: You read both passages and explain the unresolved condition, after which the newer worker says she has been using the desk aid too. Your supervisor begins taking notes, and the lead worker prepares to answer the question now connected to specific wording and a caller’s request.

feedback.text: You named what you saw, why it matters and what you need, and you were honest about what you do not know. That gives the team something to check instead of something to defend. Build on it: keep the caller’s question in view, because it shows the gap is not just a reading preference.

The newer worker has now added her own use of the desk aid to the discussion. That observable contribution matters without establishing how safe she feels or predicting whether she will raise another question.

choices.text: Keep it out of the huddle and message the lead worker afterward. The desk aid is his, and a private note is more respectful than correcting him in front of twelve people.
choices.consequence: You note your intention to write privately, while the lead worker announces that the team will use the desk aid during the renewal push. After agreeing to take additional renewals, the newer worker asks whether its income-proof line is still current before the huddle moves on.

feedback.text: A private route can be useful, but it needs timely follow-through when the shared tool is already in use. Here, a future message alone does not arrange a review or clarify what workers should do before further requests go out.
The newer worker just asked the question you were holding, with less standing to ask it. Your silence did not protect her from the risk; it left her to carry it alone.
When a shared tool is in use right now, try raising the work question in the room and keeping anything personal for later: “One line in the desk aid may not match the manual. Can someone check it?”

choices.text: Tell the huddle that the desk aid is wrong on income proof and has been sending people the wrong requests, so everyone should stop using it until someone fixes it.
choices.consequence: Several colleagues stop typing, and the lead worker asks sharply which cases support your claim that the desk aid has caused incorrect requests. You cannot yet identify which renewals fall under the manual condition, and the newer worker does not add anything to the exchange.

feedback.text: Your concern was real, but the claim went further than your evidence. Compare “the desk aid is wrong” with “these two lines read differently, and I may be missing a condition.” The second invites a check; the first invites a defense.
When something might affect callers, it is natural to sound certain so people will listen. Neither overstating your certainty nor dismissing yourself makes the evidence stronger.
When you raise a gap, how often do you say out loud what you have not yet determined?

choices.text: Stay quiet for now. The lead worker has far more experience, the manual may have a condition you missed, and a mistaken question in front of your supervisor would not look good.
choices.consequence: The huddle turns to queue numbers before your supervisor asks whether anyone has another question and the lead worker begins closing. The newer worker then says that a caller raised the same issue yesterday, leaving her unsure which information to provide.

feedback.text: Worrying about looking unprepared in front of a supervisor is one of the most common reasons people hold back an ordinary work question. That cost is real. The question can still be legitimate while you are unsure of the answer.

A specific question can identify the unresolved condition without claiming the answer: “These two lines read differently. Who can confirm?” That supplies information the team can examine, although no phrasing guarantees a supportive response.
The newer worker has raised the concern without hearing your similar observation. Sharing relevant evidence could support the inquiry without assuming what she felt about the earlier silence.

decisions.setup: The income-proof question reaches the huddle, and the lead worker replies, “That line has worked for two years. Everyone else understands it.” Someone laughs while the newer worker remains muted, and your supervisor glances at the clock as the waiting queue grows. The response has not established how the two instructions relate or what the team should do about the unresolved question.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: Say, “It may well be fine. Can I paste both lines in the chat?” Then ask your supervisor who confirms which condition applies, and what to use this afternoon.
choices.consequence: After you paste both passages, the lead worker says the manual may have changed since he prepared the desk aid. Your supervisor agrees to seek confirmation from the person or area responsible for policy interpretation and report back at the next huddle. She asks workers to bring unresolved cases through the established review procedure before sending a request based on an unconfirmed interpretation. When the newer worker asks about earlier letters, your supervisor offers to review the potentially affected cases with her through that procedure.

feedback.text: You returned attention to the passages and asked both who confirms the interpretation and how to handle work while it remains unresolved. Following the established review procedure keeps the question connected to current cases without inventing an interim eligibility rule.
The lead worker revisited the wording after seeing the comparison. That change is observable; whether he felt embarrassed, reassured or defensive is not established by the exchange.
Keep a short version ready for the next time a question gets laughed off: “Can we look at the actual line?” It returns attention to the work without taking on the person.

choices.text: Leave the line for now and message the newer worker privately: tell her it was a fair question and that she should not let the laugh stop her from asking.
choices.consequence: The newer worker replies with thanks, while the lead worker moves to queue planning without resolving the question about the income-proof requirement. Your private message acknowledges her concern, but neither of you has confirmation about which instruction applies to the afternoon’s renewals.

feedback.text: Your message acknowledges the colleague’s question, but the work still needs an answer. Helping the concern reach review addresses that separate need without treating private encouragement as a substitute.
When you support a colleague privately after a dismissal, what keeps the work question from being raised again in the room?

choices.text: Say that this is not the first time questions get laughed off in this huddle, and that the lead worker needs to be more open when people raise problems.
choices.consequence: The lead worker replies, “I didn’t laugh at anyone,” and two colleagues begin speaking about what happened during earlier huddles. Your supervisor says time is running out, while the group has not compared the passages or identified a route for the interpretation question.

feedback.text: The discussion has shifted toward past interactions before resolving the two passages. Returning to that comparison can advance the immediate task, while any concern about a pattern of conduct retains its appropriate reporting route.

The lead worker has disputed the description of the interaction. That response does not establish his motives or settle whether a conduct concern exists; keep the evidence about the instruction available for review.
If a pattern needs naming, try your supervisor afterward, with specifics: what was asked, what the reply was, what was left open.

choices.text: Thank the lead worker for the context, call it a great question, and ask him to look at the line next week, then move on to the queue.
choices.consequence: The lead worker agrees to look next week, and the discussion returns to the queue without anyone examining the two passages. For the afternoon, the desk aid remains in use and the unresolved condition has no confirmed review or interim instruction.

feedback.text: Smoothing a tense moment is a common and generous instinct. A polite thank-you followed by no examination can look welcoming while leaving the issue untouched.

Praise without a check sends a mixed message: asking is welcome, but nothing happens when you do. A look next week comes after this afternoon’s renewals have gone out. The stronger choice keeps the thanks and adds the comparison now.

decisions.setup: Later that afternoon, you review your own records and identify six renewals on which you used the desk aid wording last week. One belongs to this morning’s caller, but you have not yet established which cases fall under the manual condition in question. Your supervisor has an opening at two, providing an opportunity to identify the potentially affected cases and ask how to proceed.
decisions.prompt: What do you do about your own six cases?

choices.text: Bring your supervisor the six case numbers, what you requested and what the manual page says. Ask what each case now needs and who decides, and offer to make the calls.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor reviews the six case references in the authorized case system and thanks you for identifying a possible effect on prior requests. She sends the relevant information through the established policy-review route, explaining that the applicable conditions must be confirmed before deciding which requests need correction. Together, you check the procedure for pending deadlines and caller updates, rather than assuming that raising a question suspends a requirement. You contact this morning’s caller with the authorized update and agreed follow-up time, without promising a particular eligibility outcome or disclosing other cases.

feedback.text: You identified the possible error with case-specific evidence and asked who can determine the required correction. Offering to help with authorized follow-up retains responsibility for your work without assuming that you can decide eligibility requirements yourself.

The supervisor now has the relevant cases and unresolved condition available through an authorized channel. This supports a specific review without requiring personal case information to be discussed in a general team huddle.
What made it easier, or harder, to bring your own six cases than to raise the desk aid line this morning?

choices.text: Send the six people corrected requests yourself today, using the manual page’s wording. The fix is in your hands, it helps them sooner, and it does not need to become a team issue.
choices.consequence: You send six revised requests before the applicable conditions are confirmed, intending to correct the earlier wording without another review. In this fictional case, the later interpretation shows that the manual passage applies only to some renewals, leaving two revised requests incorrect. Your supervisor learns about the affected cases when a caller asks why two different letters arrived without an explanation.

feedback.text: Wanting to fix your own error quickly is a good instinct. The trouble is that the fix depended on the same open question as the desk aid. Bringing the list to your supervisor would have tied your six cases to the answer instead of guessing ahead of it.
To a caller, two different letters in a week can feel like nobody knows what they need. Quiet fixing can multiply that.
Before you correct work that depends on an open question, ask: “Does my fix rely on an answer nobody has given yet?”

choices.text: Hold off on raising your six cases until the desk aid question is settled. If the desk aid turns out to be right, there is nothing to report and no reason to raise an alarm.
choices.consequence: The six potentially affected cases remain outside the review while you wait, and two callers submit the proof originally requested. The later interpretation confirms that those renewals require different proof, so the callers receive another request after responding to the first. This morning’s caller makes a further call about the unresolved instructions, adding another contact without receiving the needed clarification.

feedback.text: Waiting until you are sure is one of the most common responses to discovering your own possible mistake. A mistake needs a present response, not only a future lesson.
If a colleague had found six of your cases before you did, what would you have wanted them to do?

choices.text: Raise it at the next huddle as a lesson for everyone: say you made the same mistake on six cases and apologize, so others feel able to admit theirs too.
choices.consequence: At the next huddle, two colleagues thank you for discussing the possible mistake, and one says she will review her own letters. The six cases have not yet reached case review, however, and this morning’s caller still has the original request without clarification. The discussion prompts another worker to examine her records but does not itself establish which requests require correction or arrange that work.

feedback.text: The discussion prompted a colleague to examine her letters, but it did not resolve the current requests. Arrange the present review and authorized correction, then discuss the learning without disclosing private case details.
Try doing both, in order: bring the case list to your supervisor today, then share what you learned at the huddle, once the people affected are taken care of.

decisions.setup: The huddle has not ended, and the income-proof question has been raised without the team comparing the desk aid and manual. The lead worker is about to respond, while you have the relevant passages available and about a minute to add context. Consider how to identify the uncertainty without claiming that every request made from the desk aid was necessarily incorrect.
decisions.prompt: What do you add?

choices.text: Unmute and add what you found: the desk aid line, the current manual page and the caller’s question. Say you may be missing a condition, and ask who can confirm.
choices.consequence: You identify both passages and the caller’s question, then explain that the applicable condition still needs confirmation from the responsible reviewer. The newer worker says she noticed the same difference, and the lead worker prepares to respond with the wording now available.

feedback.text: You supplied the passages and identified what remains unknown, giving the reviewer a specific issue to examine. Follow through on the response rather than assuming that clear evidence always persuades everyone immediately.
The newer worker can refer to the same passages when describing her concern. Comparing them makes the work question clearer without determining anyone’s responsibility before the review.

choices.text: Say the line seems worth a second look, but leave the manual page out, so the question does not feel like a pile-on against the person who wrote it.
choices.consequence: You support another look without supplying the manual passage, so colleagues still cannot compare the wording that prompted your concern. The lead worker begins answering without that source in front of the team, leaving the specific difference unexplained.

feedback.text: Keeping the tone gentle matters. But a feeling without the page leaves the team with something to weigh rather than a line to compare. The manual page was the most useful thing you had.
When you soften a question to avoid a pile-on, what do you leave out, and who pays for it later?

choices.text: Let the lead worker handle it. The question is out now, and adding your manual page might look like you are building a case against the person who wrote the desk aid.
choices.consequence: You remain muted as the lead worker begins responding, while the manual passage on your screen has not been shared. The team hears the concern without the comparison that could help distinguish a conflicting instruction from a condition that applies differently.

feedback.text: Not wanting to pile on a colleague is a fair concern. Another way to see the choice: you can amplify a dismissal or help the work question be heard, even when you are not the decision-maker.
Offer evidence as help, not a case: “Here’s the page I was looking at, in case it’s useful.”

decisions.setup: The huddle is about to close without comparing the two lines, while the newer worker is scheduled to process renewals this afternoon. Your supervisor remains on the call and can help route the interpretation question and clarify the procedure for unresolved cases. The team still needs to know what action is authorized before anyone relies on either passage as a complete answer.
decisions.prompt: How do you keep the question from closing with the huddle?

choices.text: Ask your supervisor directly: “Can the income-proof line go to whoever confirms policy, and can the team know which line to use this afternoon until the answer comes back?”
choices.consequence: Your supervisor agrees to route both passages for policy interpretation and asks workers to use the established review procedure for unresolved cases. She explains how the team will receive the confirmed answer and who can clarify what action is authorized in the meantime. The lead worker agrees to the check, while the interpretation itself remains unresolved and no change to eligibility requirements has been assumed.

feedback.text: You asked for a route to confirmation and clarification of what action is authorized while the answer is pending. Check that the response reaches affected workers and cases through the established process.
The supervisor now has a specific request that connects the interpretation question to current work. Her agreement identifies a next step, while its completion still needs follow-through.

choices.text: After the huddle, send the lead worker both lines with a short, neutral note, and leave it to him to decide whether the supervisor needs to see it.
choices.consequence: The lead worker replies that he will look when he can, without naming a review time or confirming an interim instruction. The desk aid remains in use that afternoon, and the supervisor has not received the question or the possible effect on callers.

feedback.text: A neutral note with both lines is far better than nothing. The gap is timing and route: the supervisor could have set a working rule for this afternoon, and the note leaves that undone.
When a tool is in use today, copy or tell the person who can set a short-term rule, and say why: “Raising this now because renewals go out this afternoon.”

choices.text: Let it go for today. The huddle has moved on, the lead worker seemed annoyed, and pushing again in front of your supervisor could make things worse between the two of you.
choices.consequence: The huddle ends without an answer, and the newer worker messages you a minute later to ask which line she should use. You cannot provide a confirmed interpretation, so her immediate work still depends on clarification that the discussion did not arrange.

feedback.text: The newer worker’s message shows where the open question went: to the person with the least standing to settle it.
What would you need from your supervisor, or from the team, to make a second try feel less risky?

practiced: Raising a question about a shared tool with an observation, its effect on callers and a specific request
Saying what you have not yet determined, without overstating or withdrawing the concern
Returning a dismissed question to the actual line and source instead of to anyone’s manner
Supporting a newer colleague by helping her question get heard, not only by comforting her
Bringing a possible mistake forward with specifics and leaving interpretation and correction decisions with the person or area responsible
Separating the present correction from a later lesson for the team
this_week: Pick one desk aid or template you use daily and compare one line with its current source. If they differ, raise it with the line, the source and one sentence on why it matters.
The next time a question gets a reply like “everyone knows that,” ask, “Can we look at the actual line?”
If you find a possible mistake, use the authorized case system to identify what happened and what needs review. Follow the current escalation and correction procedure, including any urgent deadlines.

simulations.intro: If you work in legal services, HR, communications, training or appeals, colleagues may rely on your expertise and the documents you prepare. I have noticed an urge to explain my intentions when someone questions a draft, before asking what prompted the concern. Here, you respond to a challenge about public guidance, receive a colleague’s separate conduct concern and explain what changed after the guidance was checked.
simulations.title: The Launch Draft
simulations.learner_role: You are a communications specialist. You write public web content and the scripts for staff training about program changes. You are not a supervisor. The communications lead approves final content, and what a policy requires belongs to the person or area responsible for that policy.
simulations.background: A DHS program change takes effect in three weeks, and you have spent two weeks preparing its public webpage and staff training script. During the afternoon review, a training specialist who joined six weeks ago questions a sentence in front of the communications lead and four colleagues. You wrote the sentence carefully and feel tired, but neither the effort invested nor her length of service establishes which instruction is accurate. The update routes in this fictional program need confirmation from the person or area responsible before either draft receives final approval.

decisions.setup: The specialist reads, “Call your county to update your information,” then asks why the staff training script instead tells people to update online first. You notice an urge to refer to her limited time on the team, even though her question identifies a difference between two drafts. The communications lead and four colleagues are listening while you decide how to respond to the content she has raised.
decisions.prompt: What do you say instead?

choices.text: Ask what next step the sentence suggests to her. Then put the web sentence and the training line side by side, and ask who confirms which one the policy supports.
choices.consequence: The specialist explains that the webpage suggests calling the county is the only route, while the training script gives a different starting instruction. You display both passages and acknowledge that neither of you has confirmed which route applies under the policy. The communications lead asks you to seek clarification that day, and you explain that the check will determine whether either draft needs revision.

feedback.text: You caught the defensive sentence before it landed and asked one question first. That kept two weeks of effort from becoming the answer to a question about one sentence. You also did not agree just to smooth things over. Build on it: keep a clarifying question ready for the next time your work is questioned in a room.

A newer colleague has raised a question in front of the lead and received a concrete route for checking it. That response can support further inquiry without proving how she or the other colleagues will judge the risk of speaking up.

choices.text: Thank her for a great catch, say you will check it with the communications lead after the meeting, and move on to the training script.
choices.consequence: The specialist nods, and the group moves to the training script before comparing the instructions or identifying their policy basis. The communications lead records approval as conditional on your check, leaving a specific issue unresolved before the webpage can receive final approval.

feedback.text: Acknowledging the question is useful, but the conditional approval still depends on completing the check. Comparing the passages and identifying the review route makes that unfinished work explicit.
When you say “great question” and move on, what does the person who asked actually get?

choices.text: Explain that the sentence went through two rounds of review with the program area before she joined, so the wording is settled, and offer to walk her through the history later.
choices.consequence: The specialist says okay and looks at her notes, while two colleagues close their laptops without contributing to the question. Your account establishes that earlier review occurred, but it does not explain the different instructions or show which one applies. The reason for the other colleagues’ actions is unknown, so their silence cannot establish either agreement or a shared concern.

feedback.text: You did not say the tenure line, but this was a polite version of it. Review history and length of service cannot show whether a sentence is clear. Tenure does not determine a sentence’s meaning or accuracy.
Others heard the exchange but did not explain their own reactions. Focus on the question left unresolved rather than inferring agreement, embarrassment or a shared concern from their silence.
Defending work you invested in is one of the most human reactions there is. Noticing the urge is the first step; asking one question before explaining is the second.

choices.text: Agree right away and change the sentence to match the training script, since she is probably right and arguing over a draft in front of the team is not worth it.
choices.consequence: You begin changing the webpage to match the script until another colleague asks which route the policy actually supports. Because nobody has confirmed the answer, you stop the edit with the original inconsistency still unresolved and both instructions needing review.

feedback.text: Taking her seriously was right. Agreeing without checking is a different thing. Welcoming a question does not decide its answer; the sentence still needed its source.
Try: “Good question. I’m not sure which is right either. Let’s check it with whoever owns the policy before either version goes out.”

decisions.setup: After the review, the training specialist asks to speak privately about a separate concern involving a colleague on another team. For a month, she says, he has used a shortened name despite her requests to stop and joked that her name is too difficult. She also reports that he mocked her accent in a group chat yesterday, then asks you not to tell anyone. Consider how to respond without promising confidentiality or an outcome beyond your authority, while explaining the reporting responsibility that applies.
decisions.prompt: How do you respond?

choices.text: Thank her, explain the DHS reporting expectation and limits of confidentiality, and ask what support would help while the concern follows the appropriate route.
choices.consequence: She says she had hoped the conversation could stay private. You acknowledge that wish and explain that DHS expects employees to promptly report discrimination, harassment or retaliation complaints to a supervisor or Equal Opportunity and Access. You describe the appropriate route without deciding whether the account proves a violation. You also distinguish support from a union representative or the Employee Assistance Program from an agency report. She asks you to go with her while the concern is raised, and you agree. You keep the account factual, avoid circulating it among colleagues and do not confront the person she described.

feedback.text: You explained your responsibilities before promising privacy and kept choices about support open. Follow the appropriate reporting route without investigating or requiring proof.
She may need time to understand the process even though reporting responsibilities still apply. A clear explanation is more reliable than a promise that later has to be withdrawn.
Know where to find current reporting contacts and support options. Explain the difference so that seeking support is not mistaken for making an agency report.

choices.text: Offer to have a quiet word with the colleague yourself, peer to peer, so the name-calling stops without her having to file anything or make it into something formal.
choices.consequence: The specialist hesitates and says she is unsure whether she wants the colleague to know that she spoke with you. Your proposed private confrontation has not explained the reporting process or what can be promised about information shared through that process.

feedback.text: Wanting to stop the behavior quickly is understandable. An independent confrontation can expose her and interfere with the proper process; explain your reporting role instead.
Compare a promise to settle it yourself with an explanation of where the concern goes and what support you can offer. The second is honest about your authority.
What would help her understand the next step without promising control over an agency process?

choices.text: Say you will send the account to the agency and that the conversation is now finished, without explaining the process or asking what support she needs.
choices.consequence: She asks whether the colleague will learn that she spoke to you and what happens after the report. You have not explained your responsibilities or the limits of what you can promise. Reporting through the appropriate route is valid, but ending the conversation leaves her questions about the process and support unanswered.

feedback.text: The gap is not the decision to use an appropriate reporting route. It is closing the conversation without explaining your responsibilities, the limits of confidentiality or available support.
