Correct the known guidance problem promptly, then examine the drafting, review and approval responsibilities alongside the shared-source conditions. Learning about the system and individual accountability can proceed through their appropriate processes.

choices.text: Tell the division in your update that the policy analyst drafted from an outdated source, so everyone understands what went wrong and checks their own sources more carefully from now on.
choices.consequence: The corrected bulletin and your division update go out that day, with the update identifying the analyst’s drafting error but omitting the review and approval steps. You have not explained how the shared source was verified or whether your own approval checked its currency. The correction still needs follow-through for affected decisions, while the public attribution offers an incomplete account of how the error reached counties.

feedback.text: Naming one person’s step publicly answered who, not how. It hid the review gap and made the error about a person. Tracing the handoff would have found both.

The update singles out a drafting action while leaving later decisions out of the account. Share the process information staff need and handle personnel matters through the appropriate route rather than making a division announcement a verdict.

choices.text: Hold a learning review with the whole team next week before anything changes, so the correction to counties reflects everything it finds in one message.
choices.consequence: The county representative calls again while workers continue using the outdated guidance and your team waits for the following week’s review. The review may explain how the error occurred, but the known threshold error already requires prompt correction through the authorized route. Delay expands the period to examine for affected decisions without making the eventual explanation a substitute for that corrective work.

feedback.text: A learning review is worth doing. It cannot do the current work. The correction counties needed today did not depend on knowing how the error happened.
The county has asked for usable guidance while the state reviews the error. Explain the correction route and timing without requiring the county to wait for a complete account of the cause.

decisions.setup: During the response to the bulletin error, a temporary project staff member says he questioned the source two weeks before publication. He reports that his supervisor dismissed the warning, then made a joke about his disability when he raised it again in front of colleagues. The supervisor controls his next assignment, and he says he was unsure whom else to tell. His account raises both a work-process concern and an allegation requiring immediate reporting, regardless of how far the bulletin correction has progressed.
decisions.prompt: He has raised a work warning and a disability-related comment by his supervisor. What do you do?

choices.text: Thank him, and say you must report the disability comment to human resources this morning and will not investigate it yourself. Ask what he needs to feel safe at work.
choices.consequence: You explain the reporting duty and immediately report the allegation to DHS Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division under the agency procedure. You do not interview witnesses or approach the supervisor to resolve the allegation yourself, and you avoid promising confidentiality or a particular outcome. You ask about immediate needs, coordinate any protective measures with the responsible area and explain how to report possible retaliation. Separately, you preserve the earlier source warning for the work review without circulating allegation details in a team announcement.

feedback.text: You explained the duty, reported immediately and kept investigation with the authorized office. The earlier work warning still needs examination without exposing allegation details or interfering with that office’s process.

His temporary appointment and assignment relationship are relevant to the needs he raises. Discuss appropriate support and follow-through without promising that any one measure eliminates retaliation risk.
Do you know, today, how to reach the person in human resources who receives these reports for your area?

choices.text: Promise to keep it between the two of you and talk to his supervisor yourself, so the joke stops quickly, his assignment is protected, and nobody has to go through a formal process.
choices.consequence: He thanks you, but your promise of secrecy conflicts with the immediate reporting duty before any conversation with the supervisor has occurred. You have not yet made the required referral, and the proposed informal intervention cannot replace the agency’s authorized handling of the allegation. You need to correct the promise promptly and explain the next step without assuming his thanks means that he feels protected.

feedback.text: Wanting to protect him and fix it fast is a caring instinct. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures. A private talk cannot replace that, or come first.
An informal approach could reveal information or affect the agency’s handling of the allegation. Explain the reporting limits accurately and let the authorized office direct the next steps.

choices.text: Suggest a conversation with him and his supervisor together this week, so each can hear the other, and decide afterward whether the comment needs to go to human resources at all.
choices.consequence: He asks whether his supervisor would be in the room, and no joint conversation has yet taken place. Your proposal would make that encounter a condition before a report that you are already required to make immediately. You need to withdraw that condition and route the allegation through the agency procedure rather than decide its seriousness through an informal meeting.

feedback.text: Repair may matter later. It cannot come first, and it cannot decide whether a required report happens. The stronger move reports now and asks him what he needs.
To him, this offer means facing his supervisor before anyone with authority to act has heard what happened.

choices.text: Before deciding anything, quietly ask two people on the team whether they heard the joke, so you know what actually happened and can tell human resources something solid.
choices.consequence: You describe your plan to question colleagues, but have not yet contacted them or reported the allegation. Such questioning would begin a fact-finding process outside your role in this situation and could disclose information unnecessarily. The referral needs to happen immediately without waiting for you to corroborate the account.

feedback.text: Wanting solid facts is reasonable. Gathering them belongs to the people who receive the report. A referral does not depend on whether you believe the account.

You cannot guarantee that questioning colleagues would remain private or that protective arrangements are already in place. Report the account promptly and coordinate immediate needs through the responsible area.

decisions.setup: He is still sitting across from you. He asks, “So what happens now with what I told you about the comment?” Nothing has been reported or said to anyone yet.
decisions.prompt: He has asked what happens next. What do you tell him?

choices.text: Say you spoke too soon. You must report the comment to human resources immediately and will not look into it yourself. Ask what he needs in the meantime.
choices.consequence: You acknowledge the mistaken offer and immediately report to DHS Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division through the agency procedure. You explain that you cannot promise secrecy, a particular finding or that his supervisor will be unable to infer who raised the concern. You ask about immediate needs, coordinate appropriate measures and explain the route for reporting possible retaliation. Your correction establishes what you will do now, while the receiving office determines the next steps in its process.

feedback.text: You corrected the mistaken promise and made the required report immediately. Stay within your role, coordinate support and check in appropriately without promising the receiving office’s timing or conclusions.
An honest explanation gives him information about the next step and its limits. Ask what he needs rather than assuming how he experiences the correction of your earlier offer.

choices.text: Keep your first answer for now, and tell him you will check back with him in two weeks and report only if the joke has happened again.
choices.consequence: You tell him you will wait two weeks, leaving the allegation unreported through the required channel while no authorized assessment has begun. His thanks does not waive your duty or establish that the proposed delay protects him. The report must be made immediately rather than conditioned on another incident, and the earlier promise needs correction.

feedback.text: Trust matters, and it is why the honest answer matters. Checking back in two weeks sounds attentive, but a manager’s duty to report a protected-class comment does not wait two weeks, or for it to happen again.
Not wanting to break a confidence is a decent impulse. The duty exists so that protection does not depend on one manager’s judgment of whether a comment counts.

choices.text: Ask him whether he wants it reported. If he says no, respect that, since he knows the situation best and should stay in control of what happens to his own account.
choices.consequence: He says he needs time to think, while you have left a required report pending rather than explaining your own responsibility. His preferences matter to support and communication, but they do not waive the manager’s immediate reporting duty. DHS employees also have prompt reporting obligations under the agency policy; a coworker’s concern is not automatically exempt because the affected person prefers privacy.

feedback.text: At DHS, employees report covered concerns promptly, while supervisors and managers must report them immediately through the prescribed route. Ask about preferences for support without presenting a required report as a choice he must make.
His uncertainty does not resolve your reporting responsibility. Explain that distinction while acknowledging his concerns about assignments and how information will be handled.

decisions.setup: Ten days after the error was identified, the corrected bulletin has been issued through the authorized channel, with review of affected decisions still requiring follow-through. Your director asks how you will prevent another source-check failure and whether additional staffing is needed. The review shows unclear responsibility for verifying current sources and an early warning that did not reach the approval process. If you have not reported the disability-related allegation, that duty remains immediate; this process-improvement discussion does not replace it or establish that a formal matter is open.
decisions.prompt: What do you change, and what do you ask for?

choices.text: Add a line in each bulletin packet for open source questions, make the current-source check one named person’s job, and review after the next two bulletins whether it catches anything.
choices.consequence: You assign the current-source check and a place to record unresolved questions, with responsibility for resolving them before guidance that depends on an answer is issued. On the next bulletin, the analyst lists two questions; the checker answers one and refers the other to the person responsible for the requirement. You describe the process change without unnecessary personal details and agree to report its performance after the next two bulletins. That update does not establish completion of affected-case corrections or any allegation handling, which remain on their respective routes.

feedback.text: The change fits the gap you found: no one owned the source check. It is small, testable and has a review point. Build on it by saying, after the second bulletin, what it did and did not catch.

A process announcement can omit unnecessary identifying details, but that omission does not guarantee anonymity. Keep allegation handling separate and verify that any still-required report has actually been made.
When you fix a process, how do you check that the fix fits the gap, not just the worry?

choices.text: Add your own sign-off as a second review on every bulletin and guidance document from now on, so nothing reaches counties without a manager’s check, and ask for a position to cover the load.
choices.consequence: You add another sign-off focused on the draft, but do not define how that review will verify the current source or handle unresolved warnings. The proposal increases the review workload without showing how the added position would address the failure already identified. More review may be justified by evidence, but an additional signature alone does not demonstrate that a source mismatch will be found.

feedback.text: Specify the review task before deciding whether another approval layer or position is needed. A defined current-source check addresses the identified gap more directly than an additional signature with no verification requirement.
Adding oversight after an error is a common reflex for managers. It can look like accountability while moving responsibility away from the people closest to the work.

choices.text: Send all staff a reminder on Monday, signed by your division director, to double-check sources before any bulletin goes out and to speak up if something looks off.
choices.consequence: You distribute the director’s reminder while the source folder and responsibility for checking current requirements remain unchanged. Staff receive a general instruction to speak up, although the reported early warning still needs examination as part of the work review. The message does not identify who will act when a source question is raised or how it reaches the approving manager.

feedback.text: “Be more careful” leaves the same invisible assumption in place, and a senior signature makes it louder, not more specific. The gap was in who checks the source, and a reminder does not assign it.
An early warning was already raised in this scenario. The improvement needs to show who receives such a warning, how it is examined and how the answer reaches the person approving guidance.

choices.text: Ask supervisors to track each analyst’s errors in county guidance on a shared dashboard, so patterns show early and your division director can see which teams need more coaching.
choices.consequence: The dashboard records the analyst’s error without recording the source-folder condition, review failure or approval gap that contributed to publication. Its early count does not establish which team is more accurate, since reporting opportunities, workload and detection also affect what appears. The current-source check remains unassigned, so the new display has not yet addressed the process problem.

feedback.text: Error counts reflect both performance and the way errors are detected and reported. Examine workload, process conditions and reporting context before using person-level counts to infer quality or coaching needs.

A shared individual count can create concern about exposure, but the scenario does not establish how every analyst responds. Assess the display’s purpose and appropriate access while addressing the source-check failure.

practiced: Correcting a public-facing error first, then examining how it happened
Keeping learning about an error separate from any performance question, without erasing responsibility
Reporting a protected-class comment immediately, without investigating it yourself
Being honest about what you cannot keep confidential, and watching for retaliation
Matching a process change to the gap you found, with a review point
Keeping a private concern out of a team announcement while a formal matter is open
this_week: Pick one piece of guidance your area sends out. Write down who checks its source, by role. If no one does, name someone.
Find out who in human resources receives protected-class reports for your area, and save that contact where you can reach it quickly.
At your next managers’ meeting, when an error comes up, ask first what the people affected need today.
Tell your teams one thing that changed because someone raised a concern, after checking with that person how they want it handled.

simulations.intro: If you write policy or guidance, a small discrepancy can raise a question that needs an answer before staff rely on the draft. I have learned to state what I observed and what remains uncertain without treating careful wording as a guarantee of another person’s response. Here, you review a colleague’s bulletin, respond to a county question and report what comments actually changed.
simulations.title: The Draft Bulletin
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Program Consultant. You draft and review bulletins and guidance for counties and lead agencies, co-lead stakeholder workgroups, and carry questions to the people who decide policy. You do not approve bulletins yourself.
simulations.background: In this fictional program, a bulletin will explain a changed process for requesting a service review, with approval scheduled in three weeks. A senior consultant leads the draft, the program manager approves it, and you co-facilitate a workgroup with county staff, lead-agency staff and a disability advocate. The phone and identification conditions used in the exercise are illustrative, so actual guidance must be checked against the current requirements for the relevant program. Your role includes proposing edits and raising questions, while final approval remains with the program manager.

decisions.setup: The draft names only a web form, while the current source you are checking also lists a phone route with a condition you have not yet verified. The lead author has extensive program experience, and draft comments are due tomorrow. You have identified a possible omission, but do not yet know whether the phone route applies to this type of request.
decisions.prompt: You have found a possible gap in a senior colleague’s draft. How do you raise it?

choices.text: Comment that the paragraph names only the web form, while the current source also lists a phone line. Ask which applies here, and say you may be missing a condition.
choices.consequence: The lead author checks the source and confirms that the fictional phone route applies when a person cannot use the web form. The draft is revised to explain that condition, with the program manager’s approval still required before publication. The author thanks you for identifying the source, but the useful result is the verified clarification rather than a guarantee that this phrasing always avoids defensiveness.

feedback.text: You supplied an observation and source for verification while acknowledging what you had not determined. That made the question specific; the author remained responsible for examining it regardless of tone.
Experience can help interpret a source, but does not make the draft immune from review. A precise question supports that review without predicting whether the author will find it easy to receive.
When you doubt a senior colleague’s draft, which do you tend to do: soften the question until it disappears, or sharpen it into a charge?

choices.text: Add a light comment that says, “Probably nothing, and I may well be wrong, but is there also a phone option?” so the lead author does not feel challenged by a less senior colleague.
choices.consequence: The lead author marks the comment resolved without checking the source or changing the paragraph, so the possible omission remains unexamined. Your tentative wording did not cause an obligation to ignore it; the author still needed to assess the substantive question. You can follow up with the source location and ask for verification before the draft proceeds.

feedback.text: Softening a question to a senior colleague is very common, and care for the relationship matters. But humility does not require pretending the evidence is irrelevant. Say what you saw and what you have not determined.
Next time, try: “This paragraph names only the web form. The current source also lists a phone line. I may be missing a condition. Which applies here?”

choices.text: Raise it at the draft review meeting: say the paragraph hides the phone option from the people who most need it, so the team takes access seriously this time instead of as an afterthought.
choices.consequence: The lead author disputes the implication that information was deliberately hidden, and the meeting ends without checking the source condition. The access question remains legitimate even though your phrasing added a possible motive that the paragraph does not establish. Returning to the exact wording and source would focus the review without guaranteeing a particular reaction from the author.

feedback.text: The access concern is serious, and raising it was worth doing. “Hides” adds a motive the paragraph cannot show, and the discussion turns to defending character. The specific line and source would have carried the same weight.
The author disputed the implied motive, while the applicability question remained unanswered. Address that distinction without assuming what everyone else learned or felt during the exchange.

choices.text: Edit the paragraph in the shared draft today to add the phone line, since that is faster than a comment thread and the lead author can change it back.
choices.consequence: You add the phone route without its source condition, leaving the shared draft with a broader instruction than the fictional program source supports. The lead author asks for the basis of the change when reviewing it the next day, and the applicability question remains unresolved. Proposing an edit is within your drafting role, but an unverified change should be identified for review rather than treated as settled guidance.

feedback.text: A proposed edit can be appropriate in a shared draft. Verify its basis, flag uncertainty and follow the review process; making an edit does not grant final approval authority.
The author asked for the basis of the revision. Provide the source and clarify the unverified condition rather than assuming how the change affected confidence in the shared document.

decisions.setup: A week later, the workgroup meets by video. The county representative asks, “On the new request form, the state ID field is marked required. What happens to someone who doesn’t have one? Do they just get stuck?” Before you answer, your co-facilitator says, “That’s covered in the FAQ on the website. You should have read it.” The county representative goes quiet. You know the FAQ mentions ID but does not say what happens without one.
decisions.prompt: A partner’s question has been met with a rebuke. What do you do?

choices.text: Say the FAQ mentions ID but not what happens without one. Say you will take it to the person responsible for the form requirements and report back before the bulletin closes.
choices.consequence: You acknowledge that the FAQ does not answer the question and refer it to the person responsible for the form, with a status update before bulletin approval. The county representative and advocate describe examples without sharing unnecessary personal details, and your co-facilitator records the unresolved issue. You also discuss the dismissive reply with your co-facilitator through the appropriate working relationship rather than treating referral alone as repair. If the answer is delayed, the program manager must assess its effect on approval instead of relying on an unsupported form instruction.

feedback.text: You answered the question’s substance, admitted what the FAQ does not cover, and gave the question a route and a return. You did not promise the field would change. Build on it by bringing back the answer, whatever it is.
The county representative supplied additional evidence after the gap was acknowledged. Follow through on that evidence without claiming the exchange determines what future questions will cost her.
When a partner asks something you think is answered somewhere already, how do you check whether that answer is usable?

choices.text: Jump in warmly: tell the county representative it is a great question, that you will check who owns the ID field and report back after approval, and move to the next item.
choices.consequence: The county representative thanks you, but you have offered only a check after approval and have not corrected the claim that the FAQ answers her question. The issue may require a later correction or amendment, but it has no defined route into the current approval decision. A warmer response does not establish that the concern has been resolved or that the earlier exchange no longer matters.

feedback.text: The response acknowledged the question but left its timing outside the current approval process. Bring the issue to the program manager before approval and keep partners informed of any delay.
A supportive tone can help a discussion, but does not itself resolve a substantive gap or a dismissive response. Address both through appropriate follow-through.

choices.text: Turn to the disability advocate and ask whether the people she works with usually have a state ID, so the workgroup hears from someone who knows the community before deciding what to do.
choices.consequence: The advocate describes variation among people she has worked with and explains the limits of that experience. That information may help identify barriers, but it does not determine what the form requires or how a person without identification can proceed. The county question still needs an answer from the responsible program area, without making the advocate’s account stand for everyone.

feedback.text: Hearing from people with direct knowledge is useful. Asking one person to speak for a community is not, and it does not answer whether the field must be required. The person responsible for the requirement can.
Her account is useful within its stated limits. Do not turn a contribution based on experience into responsibility for establishing a program requirement or representing a whole group.

choices.text: Tell the workgroup you will have the ID field dropped from the required list in the final form, so partners see right away that their input changes things.
choices.consequence: After the meeting, the program manager explains that you cannot authorize removal of the identification requirement and refers the question for verification. You now need to correct your promise promptly, explaining what is being checked and when partners will receive a status update. Their response to that correction is not established, and the form requirement remains unresolved.

feedback.text: Showing partners that input matters is the right aim. Promising a change you cannot authorize, before anyone checks the requirement, spends trust you will need later.
Correct the promise before partners rely on it and explain the verification route. You cannot determine in advance whether they prefer that response or how it affects their confidence.

decisions.setup: A few minutes later, still in the meeting, the county representative unmutes. “Sorry to come back to this, but I’m still not sure what happens to the person without an ID. Who would know, and will we hear before the bulletin goes out?” Your co-facilitator glances at the clock.
decisions.prompt: The county representative has asked again. What do you say?

choices.text: Thank her for asking again. Say the FAQ doesn’t cover it, that you will take it to the person responsible for the form, and bring the answer to the next meeting.
choices.consequence: You acknowledge that the FAQ does not answer the question, refer it for verification and commit to updating the next meeting before approval. The county representative says that helps, and the advocate asks to receive the answer as well. You identify how to escalate a delayed or material answer to the program manager, without promising that the field will change. The second request has exposed a gap in your earlier response that still needs reliable follow-through.

feedback.text: You treated the second ask as a signal about your first answer, not as an interruption, and you gave the question a person and a date. Build on it by naming the owner and date the first time, so no one has to ask twice.
The county representative has had to repeat an unanswered question. Give an accurate status and reliable return rather than assuming that thanks alone makes future participation easier.

choices.text: Offer to talk with her after the meeting so the workgroup can stay on its agenda, since one county’s situation may not be what the rest of the group needs to hear about.
choices.consequence: The county representative agrees to speak afterward, and you refer the question following that conversation. No plan has been made to return the general answer to the workgroup, although others have identified the same issue. The private discussion can be useful for details, but the shared requirement still needs a suitable update before the bulletin’s approval.

feedback.text: A follow-up conversation can help. This question affects every county using the form, and the workgroup is where its answer belongs.
Which questions in your workgroups get moved offline, and who never hears their answers?

choices.text: Share the FAQ link in the chat and suggest she read the section on identification, then send any remaining questions by email so you can look at them properly.
choices.consequence: She acknowledges the link, then emails the unanswered question that afternoon, and the program manager refers it to the person responsible for the form. The referral has now occurred, but your response in the meeting did not identify the FAQ’s gap or establish a return date. You still need to correct the account of what the FAQ answers and report the verified result to the workgroup.

feedback.text: The FAQ may answer a different question. Pointing to it again does not show whether she could find or use what she needed; asking about her specific question does.
The repeated link did not answer the question she asked. Acknowledge that limitation without interpreting her brief response as acceptance or assigning feelings to her.

decisions.setup: The program manager has approved two wording suggestions and declined a shorter timeline because its governing requirement is outside this program’s authority to alter. Those decisions do not establish that any phone-route problem left earlier has been resolved; it still requires verification if unaddressed. The identification question has been referred to the person responsible for the form and remains unanswered, including after any promise you made to remove the field. Your co-facilitator drafts a thank-you for fourteen comments claiming that all concerns have been addressed, while the bulletin is still awaiting final approval.
decisions.prompt: What do you send the workgroup?

choices.text: Rewrite it to name the two wording changes and the comments behind them, why the timeline suggestion was not adopted, and that the ID question is still open.
choices.consequence: You identify the two approved wording changes, explain the governing limit on the timeline and distinguish each unresolved question from completed review. You correct any unsupported promise about the identification field and give the responsible contact and next status date, including what happens if the answer is delayed. The program manager receives the unresolved issues before deciding whether the bulletin can proceed, while partners receive the same substantive account without unnecessary personal information. Some may disagree with the decisions; an accurate update does not require or establish their endorsement.

feedback.text: You showed what changed because people spoke up, what did not and why, and what is still open. A declined suggestion with a reason is part of follow-through, not a failure of it. Build on it by sending the ID answer when it comes, even if partners hoped for a different one.
A specific account lets partners check how their comments were understood and used. It can support scrutiny even when they disagree with a decision or identify another unresolved issue.

choices.text: Keep the update short and positive: thank everyone for their 14 comments, say the bulletin is stronger for them, and save the details of what changed for the bulletin itself.
choices.consequence: The message thanks members but does not identify the adopted changes, reasons for declining the timeline suggestion or the unresolved identification question. Members would have to compare the final bulletin with their comments to infer what happened, and that comparison would not explain the pending requirement. The update has omitted relevant status information regardless of whether recipients appreciate the thanks.

feedback.text: A count of comments is activity, not an account of influence. Partners need to know what happened to their own input, including the parts that were not adopted.
Keeping partner updates brief and upbeat is a common habit. Upbeat is fine; vague is the problem.

choices.text: Send your co-facilitator’s draft as written. Every comment was considered by the program manager, the bulletin is close to final, and the ID question will likely be settled before partners notice.
choices.consequence: The county representative replies, “Addressed how? The ID question isn’t answered.” Others in the workgroup read her reply. The update claimed more than the record shows, and the first person to say so is the one who was rebuked at the meeting.

feedback.text: “Considered” and “addressed” are different. One question is still open, and saying otherwise invited exactly the reply you got.
The county representative has challenged a completion claim with a specific unresolved question. Correct the status and follow through without claiming to know how every member views the next update.

choices.text: Hold the update until the program manager approves the bulletin and the ID answer arrives, so partners get one complete, final account instead of a partial one.
choices.consequence: You delay the update while decisions already made remain unreported and the identification question is still pending. The workgroup does not receive a chance to identify misunderstandings before the scheduled approval, unless the process is changed. Later correction remains possible, but it does not replace giving the program manager and contributors an accurate account of current uncertainty.

feedback.text: Report settled decisions and open questions now, with the next review date and the implications for approval. A later final account cannot substitute for information needed at the current decision point.
How long do partners usually wait to hear what happened to their input, and what do they conclude in the meantime?

practiced: Raising a gap as an observation, a reader consequence and a question, with honest uncertainty
Staying firm about a gap without adding a motive or taking over someone else’s decision
Receiving a partner’s question after a rebuke, and giving it a person and a date
Not asking one person to speak for a whole community
Reporting back what changed, what did not and why, and what is still open
this_week: The next time you doubt a draft, write your comment in three parts: what you saw, what it could mean for a reader, and what you need checked.
In your next workgroup, when someone points to a website or FAQ as the answer, check whether it answers the question that was asked.
Look at your last update to a workgroup or partner group. Does it say what happened to anyone’s actual comment?
Name who holds each open question from your current project, and when partners will hear back.

simulations.intro: If you supervise a team, your response to a question or mistake provides evidence of what happens when someone raises a concern. I have learned to examine the work itself while taking responsibility for how the discussion is handled. Here, you respond to conflicting templates, an incorrect reply and a challenge to your plan for reducing a backlog.

the team member who pushes back

simulations.title: The Shared Inbox
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Supervisor with eight staff. Your team answers policy questions from county and lead-agency case managers through a shared inbox. You run a daily huddle, hold one-to-ones, assign the inbox and decide how team time is used.
simulations.background: The team answers from a set of standard reply templates. A newer team member joined two months ago. A senior team member has been on the team for years and wrote many of the templates. The inbox is behind, and your manager has asked you to bring the backlog down this month. Once a week, the team takes an hour to talk through hard questions before answering them; this is the team’s own practice.

decisions.setup: In the morning huddle, the newer team member identifies two service-change templates that give different sequences for a form and a notice. The senior team member laughs, says everyone else understands the process and tells him to stop overthinking it, while two colleagues smile. The newer colleague looks down at his notes, and the template question has not been answered.
decisions.prompt: You run the huddle. What do you do in the next minute?

choices.text: Ask him which two lines he means, then ask the senior team member which order applies. If it is still unclear, send it to whoever is responsible for the templates.
choices.consequence: He identifies the lines, and the senior colleague acknowledges that one template was written for an earlier process without confirming the current sequence. You refer the conflict to the person responsible, explain how the answer will return to the team and use the established escalation route for replies needing immediate guidance. One colleague reports having answered the question both ways, which adds a possible correction task rather than proving how many replies were affected. The work question is now being examined, while the dismissive comment still warrants appropriate supervisory follow-through.

feedback.text: You examined the conflict rather than treating the colleague’s experience as proof that the templates were consistent. Return the verified answer to staff and address the dismissive comment through appropriate supervisory follow-through.

The senior colleague’s experience helped identify an older template, but the current process still required verification. Experience can inform that review without excusing a dismissive response to a question.
On your team, whose questions get answered, and whose get compared to “everyone else”?

choices.text: Move the huddle along to stay on time, then talk privately with the senior team member this afternoon about how the comment came across, so no one is embarrassed.
choices.consequence: You move to the next item, leaving the template conflict unanswered until the planned private conversation later that day. That conversation may address the senior colleague’s conduct, but no interim instruction has been given for replies that depend on the disputed sequence. The newer colleague writes in his notes; that action does not reveal what he thinks about your response.

feedback.text: Not wanting to embarrass anyone in public is considerate, and a private word may still help. But the question itself was left unanswered, and the team saw that.

Return to the conflicting lines and arrange verification while also addressing conduct appropriately. A private conversation about the comment does not replace guidance for the team’s pending replies.

choices.text: Smile, say he will pick it up with time, and pair him with the senior team member for a week so he learns the templates the way the team uses them.
choices.consequence: The newer colleague nods when you arrange the pairing, but neither template has been checked against the current process. Learning from an experienced colleague could be useful, yet it does not establish which of these conflicting instructions the team should use. The arrangement also leaves the dismissive comment unaddressed and requires him to work with the person who made it.

feedback.text: Pairing can help a newcomer. Here it turned a gap in the templates into a gap in him. The templates still disagree.

The pairing has not answered the question he brought, and his nod does not establish agreement or confidence. Check the instructions and how the working arrangement proceeds without assuming his reaction.

choices.text: Tell the senior team member, in front of everyone, that the comment was disrespectful, then ask the newer team member to repeat his question so the team can hear it properly.
choices.consequence: You name the comment as disrespectful and invite the newer colleague to repeat his question, but he does not respond immediately. The senior colleague also remains silent, leaving the template conflict unresolved at this point in the huddle. Naming the conduct was not itself the error; you still need to examine the work without depending on either person’s willingness to speak next.

feedback.text: A clear response to disrespect can be appropriate in the moment. Keep the correction proportionate, then examine the work without requiring the newer colleague to perform the repair for you.

You can read the two lines yourself and invite relevant evidence without insisting that either colleague speak immediately. Addressing the comment and resolving the template conflict are both supervisory responsibilities.

decisions.setup: Before the huddle ends, the newer team member says to leave it for now, without explaining why he no longer wants to discuss it. The conflicting templates remain available for afternoon replies, and you have a few minutes to address that work problem. You can do so without requiring him to explain his feelings or continue speaking in front of colleagues.
decisions.prompt: He has withdrawn his question. What do you do with the minutes left?

choices.text: Say you let his question get brushed past and want to return to it now. Ask which two lines he meant, and who here answers that kind of question most.
choices.consequence: You acknowledge that the question was left unresolved and put the two lines where the team can examine them without requiring a personal explanation. Colleagues identify conflicting replies, which you refer to the person responsible for the templates along with the question about the current sequence. You direct urgent inquiries through the established escalation route while clarification is pending, rather than assuming a paused reply suspends any required deadline. You tell the team when to expect an update and follow through on any correction identified by that review.

feedback.text: You acknowledged the unresolved question and took responsibility for its review. Bring back the verified answer and check any affected replies rather than treating referral alone as completion.
You do not know why he withdrew from the discussion. You can respect that choice while continuing to examine the instructions and offering an appropriate private check-in.

choices.text: Take him at his word for now and check in with him privately tomorrow morning; pushing a newer person to keep going in front of the team could embarrass him more.
choices.consequence: The huddle ends without a check of the conflicting instructions, and staff continue using both templates that afternoon. Your planned private check-in may help you understand his experience, but the work now also needs review for incorrect replies and any required corrections. The afternoon’s messages cannot be unsent, although appropriate follow-up can still correct information supplied to case managers.

feedback.text: Respecting his wish not to be pushed is thoughtful, and a check-in can still help. But his question was about the templates, not about him. You could have reopened the work without putting him back on the spot.
Next time, try: “I let that get brushed past. Let’s look at the two lines now; they go out this afternoon.”

choices.text: Tell the team your door is always open and no question is a bad question, so the newer team member knows he can bring anything to you privately.
choices.consequence: Several colleagues nod at your invitation, while the conflicting templates remain available and no one is assigned to obtain the current sequence. A private route for questions can be useful, but this invitation does not answer the issue already raised in the huddle. You have not yet told the team how to handle replies that depend on the unresolved instructions.

feedback.text: An open-door statement is only as good as the response behind it. The huddle just showed what happens to a question; a speech does not change that, but answering it would.
How many questions have come through your open door this month, and what might that number not tell you?

decisions.setup: Two days later, a respected team member reports that she sent an old contact step last week without checking it against the current source. The case manager has already shared that step with two families, and the employee asks how to correct the reply. This is a separate template problem; any unresolved sequence question from the huddle still needs its own follow-through.
decisions.prompt: She has brought you her own mistake. What do you do?

choices.text: Thank her for bringing it. Ask her to send the case manager a correction today for the two families, then look together at how the old step reached her reply.
choices.consequence: She sends a correction to the case manager, who agrees to pass it to the two families; delivery to those families still needs confirmation. Together you find similarly named old and current templates, and you ask the responsible person to retire the outdated copy from active use under the records procedure. You agree how staff will verify the current source and check whether other replies used the old step. You acknowledge her report without promising that reporting removes accountability or assuming the full effect of the error is already known.

feedback.text: You began the correction and examined the template process. Confirm the authorized follow-up reached the affected families, and check that outdated instructions are no longer available for active use.

Thanking her acknowledges the value of reporting, while clear correction steps maintain responsibility for the work. Follow the applicable personnel process without treating self-reporting as either automatic misconduct or immunity.
What happens on your team to the person who reports their own mistake first?

choices.text: Tell her warmly that mistakes don’t matter here and that you would rather she bring you ten errors than hide one. The template update next month will take care of the old step.
choices.consequence: You offer reassurance but do not arrange a correction for the case manager or the two families who received the old contact step. The planned template update is several weeks away, leaving the outdated copy available for another reply in the meantime. Your encouragement to report mistakes therefore needs immediate follow-through on the information and process that caused this one.

feedback.text: Wanting her to feel safe bringing errors is the right aim, and relief is a fair thing to offer. But this mistake does matter: two families have the old step. Safety is not a lower standard; it is making the standard safe to meet.
Thank her for reporting and arrange a prompt correction, then examine the shared template problem. That response addresses the error without assuming how relieved she will feel.

choices.text: Thank her, then write it up as a performance note so her record is accurate, and remind her to check templates against the current source before sending any reply.
choices.consequence: You create a performance note and remind her to check sources, but do not discuss correcting the reply already shared with the families. The old template remains available, and you have not examined whether the same problem affected other staff or replies. Whatever documentation the personnel process requires, it does not replace timely correction or a review of the conditions that contributed to the error.

feedback.text: Apply the appropriate personnel and records requirements based on the facts, while correcting affected work and examining the process. Psychological safety does not prohibit necessary documentation or make every self-reported error a disciplinary matter.
The note records an individual error while leaving the shared source problem untouched. Examine both the employee’s action and the conditions that made an outdated template easy to use.

choices.text: Plan to walk the team through her mistake at the next team meeting, step by step, so everyone learns to check their templates, and let her know it’s coming.
choices.consequence: She asks you not to make her mistake the subject of the planned meeting, while the case manager still needs a correction for the families. You have not yet addressed the outdated template, and the next team meeting is a week away. A discussion of the process may be useful, but its timing and scope need to protect relevant privacy and avoid delaying the current correction.

feedback.text: Team learning from an error can be valuable. It does not come before the current correction, and it does not need her at the center. The old copy in the template folder is the lesson.

A supervisor may need to share relevant lessons, but should avoid unnecessary identification, blame or disclosure. Discuss the process in a way that supports learning while following the applicable privacy and personnel requirements.

decisions.setup: At the next team meeting, you propose converting the weekly hour for difficult questions into inbox time for the rest of the month. A team member says that the discussion catches mistakes before replies go out and asks you to reconsider losing that opportunity. Your manager requested a smaller backlog, while the choice of how to use this team routine is yours to examine. Any unresolved template questions or incorrect replies from the earlier decisions remain responsibilities to address, regardless of the schedule you choose.
decisions.prompt: A team member has disagreed with your plan in front of the team. How do you respond?

choices.text: Thank him for saying it in the room. Ask what he has seen come out of that hour, explain the backlog pressure, and say you will decide by Friday.
choices.consequence: He describes two errors caught during the discussion hour last month, and another colleague explains how it helps her understand the templates. You weigh that information against the backlog and decide by Friday to retain thirty minutes, explaining your reasoning to the team and your manager. You set a review of reply quality and backlog progress rather than assuming the shorter discussion will achieve both aims. The explanation makes your decision visible without requiring agreement or treating the earlier correction tasks as finished.

feedback.text: You treated disagreement with your plan as information, and you kept the decision yours. The plan changed partway, and you said why. Build on it by checking at month’s end whether the shorter time still catches what the full hour did.

The team and your manager receive the evidence and reasoning behind the revised schedule. That explanation supports scrutiny of the decision without guaranteeing agreement or confidence in the outcome.
Where on your team is there still time to think, and to say no?

choices.text: Agree on the spot to keep the full hour, so the team sees that disagreeing with you changes things, and tell your manager the backlog will take longer than planned.
choices.consequence: You keep the full hour and tell your manager the backlog may take longer, without first checking its contribution or examining other ways to reduce the queue. The team has an immediate answer, but you have supplied little evidence about the trade-off or how its effects will be assessed. Agreement with a challenge is possible; the missing work is the examination supporting your decision.

feedback.text: Showing that disagreement can change things is valuable. Agreeing before you know what the hour catches skips the evidence. A reasoned decision, even a partial one, shows the same thing more credibly.
Leaders sometimes give way quickly to show openness. Safety and standards go together: a challenge deserves examination, not automatic agreement.

choices.text: Say the team meeting is not the place to question a plan your manager asked for, and offer him a one-to-one on Friday if he still has concerns.
choices.consequence: He acknowledges your response and does not schedule the offered one-to-one, while you convert the discussion hour into inbox time. You have not examined the concern about reply accuracy or established another way for the team to review difficult questions. His decision not to meet does not resolve the work concern or prove why he chose not to pursue that conversation.

feedback.text: A private follow-up can be appropriate for sensitive details. Here the issue concerns a shared work routine, so give the team an account of how the concern will be examined and addressed.

The concern was relevant to the team’s work, even if the meeting had limited time. Set a route and time for examining it rather than presenting the manager’s backlog request as a prohibition on questions.

choices.text: Thank him, say his point is noted and you will think about it, then convert the hour to inbox time as planned, since the decision has to be made this week.
choices.consequence: You thank him and proceed with the schedule change, without explaining whether you examined his concern or why you retained the original plan. Staff therefore have no account of how reply accuracy will be protected when the discussion hour is removed. An unchanged decision could be justified, but acknowledgment alone does not provide that justification or show what follow-up will occur.

feedback.text: A polite thank-you followed by no examination can look welcoming while leaving the issue untouched. You might still convert the hour. Saying why, after asking what it catches, makes the decision credible.
Next time, try: “I hear you. What has the hour caught lately? I’ll decide by Friday and tell you why.”

practiced: Turning a dismissed question back to the work, without making anyone the lesson
Naming your own part when you let a question get brushed past, and reopening it
Correcting a mistake for the people affected first, then looking at how it happened
Applying appropriate documentation and privacy requirements while examining a self-reported error and the shared process
Treating disagreement with your plan as information, and explaining what you decided and why
Protecting time for thinking when the work is urgent
this_week: In your next huddle, when a question gets a quick reply, ask once: “Which line are you looking at?”
Check whether current templates are clearly identified, and ask the responsible person how outdated copies are retired under the records procedure.
Think of the last mistake someone brought you. Did they leave knowing what to fix and that bringing it was worth it?
Before you cut a team routine to save time, ask the team what it catches.

action_plan: In your next meeting, when a question gets a shortcut reply, bring it back with one sentence about the work, such as who can confirm the answer.
Before you raise a concern, write it as what you observed, how it could affect the task, and what you are asking for.
When someone questions your work, ask one clarifying question before you explain or defend.
When you find a mistake, handle what the people affected need now, then name one specific step to change.
Say once a month what changed because someone spoke up, and if nothing did, say why.
Save the current contacts for Human Resources, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, a union representative and the Employee Assistance Program.

closing.narration: The course began with a reply that referred to an earlier discussion without answering the question someone had just raised. That exchange illustrates how everyday responses can teach colleagues whether useful information will receive attention or be dismissed. Psychological safety supports candid questions, acknowledgment of mistakes and substantive disagreement alongside demanding standards and professional accountability. You can contribute by raising a precise concern, examining a question about your own work and explaining how an answer will return. When an error occurs, address the present need and then examine the conditions and choices that produced it. When your response causes harm, take responsibility within your authority and follow any reporting duties without waiting for repair. Return to the moment you considered at the beginning and identify one response you would now approach differently. Explain the reason for that change, then consider how another person would recognize it in your next working conversation.

facilitator.purpose: Help colleagues examine how a team responds when someone asks a question, acknowledges an error, raises a concern or disagrees about the work. Use the simulation to practice responses that make useful information available while maintaining professional standards and required reporting procedures. Keep discussion grounded in the fictional examples so participants can explore the decisions without disclosing personal experiences or representing a community.
delivery: Individually: each person watches the segments and works through the simulation, then brings one reflection to a team conversation.
As a team session of about 90 minutes: watch the segments together, pause for the checks, and run the simulation as a group, choosing together at each decision.
As two shorter sessions: segments one to three in the first, segments four to six and the simulation in the second, one to two weeks apart.

Use voice or chat for an online discussion, allowing time for written responses before choosing the group’s next step. This gives participants more than one way to contribute without tallying individual choices.
preparation: Watch all six segments and play the simulation at least twice, once with strong choices and once with weaker ones, so you know both recovery paths.
Pick two reflection questions per segment that fit your group.
Think of a small, low-stakes moment from your own work when you brushed off a question or held one back. You may share it to set the tone.
Share the agenda and the simulation premise a day ahead, so people who like to prepare can do so.
Know the current contacts for Human Resources, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division and the Employee Assistance Program.
If you supervise or manage, Policy 1436 requires you to report a protected-class allegation immediately to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures.

DHS policy directs supervisors to promptly refer these complaints to Equal Opportunity and Access and consult that division about the appropriate action. Do not conduct an independent inquiry before referral.

agenda.title: Opening and why it matters
steps: Welcome the group and name one thing you hope to learn from them today.
Play segment one, Why an ordinary question carries risk.
Ask the check question and take two or three answers.
notes: Ask what information the opening question could contribute to the work and what the response leaves unanswered. Keep the discussion on the exchange rather than judgments about the people involved.

agenda.title: What it is, and why the risk differs
steps: Ask pairs to name one thing psychological safety is not, and one place they have seen it confused with comfort.
Ask: in your work, what routes besides speaking in the room actually reach the person who decides?
notes: Do not ask anyone to explain why they find speaking up hard, or to speak for a group.

agenda.title: Asking, receiving and mistakes
steps: Have pairs rewrite “Nobody cares about access” as an observation, a consequence and a request.
Ask: which shortcut after a mistake is more common where you work, blame or declaring nobody is responsible?
notes: Use the practice phrases rather than real cases about identifiable people.

agenda.title: Formal routes and follow-through
steps: Ask each person to name where they would find the current contact for Human Resources and the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.
Ask: what is one thing that changed on your team because someone spoke up?
notes: If a concern surfaces, thank the person and move discussion of personal details out of the group. Explain applicable reporting responsibilities and support routes. Managers and supervisors report protected-class allegations or incidents immediately under Policy 1436 and follow agency procedures without waiting for the session to end. DHS also expects employees to promptly report discrimination, harassment or retaliation complaints to a supervisor or Equal Opportunity and Access. Do not promise secrecy or investigate the account yourself.

agenda.title: Simulation: The Monday huddle
steps: Read the setup aloud and allow time to consider the choices. Invite two or three reasons, agree on the group’s next choice through discussion, and examine its consequence and coaching.
Try at least one weaker choice on purpose to show a recovery decision.
After the last decision, read the practiced list aloud.
notes: Ask whose view was hardest to see: the newer team member, the experienced colleague, the team lead or the call-line lead.

agenda.title: Closing and commitments
steps: Ask each person to pick one action plan item to try this week, privately or out loud.

say: Consider a question that someone might hesitate to raise at work, using a fictional example if helpful. What response might the person anticipate, and what information could remain unavailable?
A courteous exchange can still leave an important question unanswered, so examine whether the response helps useful information reach a decision.
The research describes a shared belief about interpersonal risk within a team. To examine that belief in practice, consider how questions and mistakes are received over time.
Psychological safety and demanding standards can coexist when people can raise problems that need attention without being ridiculed for doing so.
An invitation to raise concerns needs follow-through: people also learn from what happens after a question reaches someone with authority to respond.
Silence alone does not establish agreement, so ask which other routes allow questions to reach the person responsible for the decision.
Try the shape: what I saw, how it could affect the work, what I am asking for.
A clarifying question can help you understand the concern before responding, but its effect depends on what you ask and how you use the answer.
Address the immediate needs of the people affected, then examine the conditions and choices that contributed to the mistake so the team can consider a change.
When your role carries more authority, take responsibility for addressing your own response rather than requiring the person affected to manage the repair.
Huddle: what is the work question, and who can answer it?
Your own mistake: who relies on this, and what do they need from you right now?
The colleague's concern: what are your reporting responsibilities, and what choices about support can you explain?
In the scenario, the team lead supervises the team, so telling him starts a report. If you supervise or manage, that duty is yours too, whoever the person reports to.
As a peer, explain the DHS employee reporting expectation and the support available. Avoid promising secrecy or treating support options as substitutes for reporting.

The experienced colleague’s response left the question unanswered, while later choices either brought it back into the work or let it disappear. What evidence and responsibilities should guide the next step?
Which moment felt most like your real job?

when_stalls: Share your own small example first: a time you brushed off a question, and what you noticed afterward.
Ask people to write for one minute before anyone speaks, then invite a few to read what they wrote.
Switch to pairs for two minutes, then ask each pair for one sentence.
Ask a concrete question: what reply have you heard that ended a question without answering it?
when_tense: If someone feels blamed: “This is about what happens to a question, not about anyone's worth.”
If someone says safety means no hard feedback: “The readings say the opposite. High safety goes with high expectations.”
If a person is asked to speak for a group: “Nobody here speaks for a whole community. Speak from your own experience if you choose to.”
Thank the person and move personal details out of the group. Explain reporting responsibilities before agreeing on a private support conversation.
If you supervise or manage, report it immediately to Human Resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow agency procedures. Do not wait for the session to end.
If you do not supervise, explain the DHS employee reporting expectation and share support routes privately. Do not promise secrecy, investigate or require proof before raising the concern.
follow_up: Two weeks later, ask the team which action plan item they tried and what they noticed.
Suggest one shared habit for a month: close each team meeting by naming one thing that changed because someone spoke up, or why nothing did.
Invite the team to look at one routine, such as an agenda or a review packet, and ask when input is due and who actually reads it.
Point people to the readings listed at the end of the course, including Edmondson's work and the respectful workplace materials.
